inline.s: The Second: Showing the Marks of the Three Contemplations — The Section on Cultivation Concluded

Third, the Function of the Three Contemplations. In what has been set forth above the marks of contemplation are clearly distinguished: one who attains the perfect faculty may straightway seize the moment and enter directly; cultivating in dependence on it, the one mind is established effortlessly and naturally. Yet there is no lack of the functions of severing delusion in shallow or deep measure and of realizing truth in higher or lower degree. Hence when Ānanda heard the preceding exoteric and esoteric instructions, he obtained right permeation and cultivation, and his body and mind were filled with joy, gaining great and abundant benefit; yet he still did not know how such cultivation and realization — not yet arrived at nirvāṇa, beginning from the ordinary person and ending at the Buddha-ground, with all the successive names and stages in between — is to be reached. Therefore he asked about the fifty-five stages of the true path of bodhi. This is meant to reveal that the perfect and wondrous contemplation-practice possesses this power to sever and to realize, this capacity to turn the ordinary into the sage; hence it is called the function of the three contemplations. But why did the World-Honored One first explain the causes of the two kinds of inverted, deluded beings, and afterward show the road of the true family through the fifty-five stages? Because the wondrous nature is perfect and luminous, the true source limpid and still: originally there is no delusion or awakening — how could there be sage or ordinary being? Only when a single thought suddenly arises do the empty flowers of the three realms riot into being; only when the inch-wide mind is stilled do the phantom shadows of the one truth wholly dissolve. This is what is meant by: arising and ceasing are named delusion — deluded, birth and death have no beginning; ceasing delusion is named truth — awakened, rebirth is instantly stilled. Yet the realm of birth and death is vast; in sum it does not go beyond the twelve classes. The road of nirvāṇa is long; in brief it is no more than fifty-five stages. In truth it is because deluding the one truth turns it into the six imaginings that the two kinds of inversion follow upon one another; and because awakening the six imaginings to their root in the one truth means that the two kinds of turning-about are so named. Therefore if you now wish to cultivate samādhi and go straight to nirvāṇa, you must first recognize the cause of this inversion; only then can you perfectly accomplish the true samādhi. Why? Because deluding true awakening so that it becomes non-awakening is therefore called ignorance; shifting the unborn so that it becomes living beings is therefore called inversion. Thus what is fundamentally unborn is born — hence there are living beings of the unborn; what is fundamentally non-abiding abides — hence there are worlds of non-abiding. So the wheel of delusion does not rest: how could the karma of birth and death ever be exhausted? Deluded thoughts do not cease: how could the world of flux ever end? Moreover, since a single thought of deluded, delusive movement can make the six imaginings spring up across the board and revolve through the twelve classes of beings, so can a single thought awakening to the unborn, with the three contemplations cultivated together, realize and attain the fifty-five stages. Seen in this light, living beings are in fact defined by the mind of the four aggregates, and the world is precisely the substance of the aggregate of form; this rests wholly on the principal recompense to reveal delusion and awakening, and belongs entirely to living beings to make plain the true and the false. This is what is meant by: it is your six faculties, and nothing else, that make you revolve in birth and death and swiftly realize the wondrous and eternal. Is this not precisely: when knowing and seeing establish a known, that is the root of ignorance; when knowing and seeing are without seeing, that is nirvāṇa? Examine the main purport closely — how could one not believe it? Yet the whole of delusion is precisely the true, and inversion is complete within the wondrous perfect true mind; the whole of the true is precisely delusion, and cultivation and realization are rooted in the original disordered imaginings. Hence the three gradual stages establish the fifty-five stages by means of them, and advance through them. Why? Because the continuity of the six faculties arises from lust and killing as its cause, and the long sinking in every suffering takes stealing and falsehood as its root. Now if one would take lasting leave of the three realms and forever pass beyond the four kinds of birth, one must utterly cut off the aiding causes, so that the right nature, hollowed out, does not issue forth; one must stop the manifest activities, so that faculties and objects meet but do not function. Then roots and dust merge and are extinguished, mind and realm are both empty, body and land are luminously clear, and self and other are perfectly realized. Thus from contemplation-practice at the start up to partial true attainment, one forever severs ignorance and ascends to wondrous enlightenment. Yet contemplation layer upon layer, investigation stage upon stage — all alike rely on the great Śūraṃgama samādhi and the wondrous gate of the three contemplations, cultivating singly and in combination in perfect practice, and entering by gradual stages. The function of the three contemplations has nothing higher than this. Accomplishment in a single lifetime lies here! Cultivation and severing are brought to their utmost; hence the text concludes by returning to contemplation of mind to finish the request. Therefore it says: all these stages are entered gradually and deeply by the vajra contemplation of the ten profound similes of the illusory, and by the pure cultivation and realization of the Tathāgatas’ vipaśyanā within śamatha.
The Third: Showing the Function of the Three Contemplations — The Section on Realizing the Fruit Concluded

Fourth, Concluding the Names of the Three Contemplations. Through all the foregoing instructions, the hearer is first made to awaken to the wondrous perfect substance of mind, and on that basis the gate of wondrous perfect practice is established; by means of this wondrous practice, perfectly cultivated, he returns to realize the wondrous perfect substance. Thus the practice of turning the back on dust and uniting with awakening being finished, the road of returning from the false to the true is made clear. Therefore Mañjuśrī asked the name of the sutra, his intent being to conclude by designating the name of the contemplation. Why? Spoken in terms of worldly truth, it shows that there is no function of grasping a thing — this is to have a name without reality; argued in terms of ultimate truth, the principle has a reality that deserves the name — this is to have both reality and name. For the meaning expounded above, whether principle, practice, cause, or fruit, is wholly perfect and interfused; and so the text that expounds it, whether teaching-marks or names and phrases, all returns to the ultimate. Because the purport of the principle is deep and profound, it cannot be exhausted in a single phrase: partial and perfect illuminate one another, and five names make the circle complete. The intent is this: the essential and wondrous Dharma-gate set forth above, if named according to its substance, is the Tathāgatagarbha mind, the one true-mark seal, the true sutra of the ocean-eye; hence it is named the Great Buddha-Crown, the Sitatapatra Uṣṇīṣa, the unsurpassed jewel seal, the pure ocean-eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions. If named according to its function, then whoever has the causal bond may receive deliverance; delusion is without exception severed, truth is without exception exhausted; hence it is named the kindred cause of rescue and protection, delivering Ānanda and the nun of the nature of the Sun-follower, enabling them to attain the bodhi-mind and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. If it points exactly to cause and fruit both being true, then the beginning of every Buddha’s fostering and accomplishment is nothing but the ultimate destination; hence it is named the Tathāgata’s secret cause, the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization. If substance and function are discussed together as vast and great, with cause and fruit simultaneous, then it contains defilement and purity without changing, is sovereign and inconceivable, possesses the virtues of the nature without omission, and brings forth the immeasurable; hence it is named the great, vast, and perfect Wondrous Lotus King, the dhāraṇī-mantra that is mother to the Buddhas of the ten directions. If one takes the middle-way words spoken from the dharmakāya, then one who accords with them at once inherits the Buddha’s family, and cultivating them never departs from the great samādhi; hence it is named the consecration chapter and the Śūraṃgama of the myriad practices of all bodhisattvas. All these name it in accordance with reality and establish titles according to its virtues; in sum they do not go beyond the one mind, and in brief they do not depart from the three contemplations. This is what is meant by: though the words ask the name of the sutra, the intent is to conclude by designating the name of the contemplation. Thus teaching, principle, practice, and fruit all return to the source of the great samādhi, and the true and the false, the awakened and the deluded, all enter the Tathāgatagarbha mind. The great cause and condition is nothing beyond this; opening, showing, awakening, and entering have nothing higher than this.
The Fourth: Concluding the Names of the Three Contemplations — Concluded

The seven and a half scrolls of text above have been given a general analysis, greatly opening the gate of cultivation and realization and setting out these four chapters, and there is good reason for it. Still, in first drafting this for beginners I was truly ignorant of its finer details; as for the broad outline, I have briefly marked the main points. I hope that those who cultivate in hidden retreat and like-minded people of high caliber will first read the sutra text thoroughly, then set their minds at ease in the contemplation, review this writing and comprehend it, and forgetting words and images, silently accord with it. May the eternal light one day appear, so that faculties, dust, and consciousness dissolve; then the Buddha-Dharma and body-and-mind will all be secondary matters. How much the more is this deluded consciousness, relying on mere inference — is it not superfluous talk?
The above: Greatly Opening the Gate of Cultivation and Realization — Concluded
Next, Subtly Showing the Differences between Delusion and Awakening:

Above, the one mind has been revealed: the true source is already penetrated, the wondrous purport of the three contemplations is greatly understood, the appearances of delusion and awakening are fully set out, and the feelings of ordinary being and sage are exhausted. Yet delusion is but a single thought: because feelings and imaginings riot forth, one takes the rise and fall of the seven destinies. Awakening stops at the one mind: because false views spring up across the board, one takes the demonic disturbances of the five aggregates. Hence it is said: the self-mind grasps the self-mind; the non-illusory becomes illusory dharmas. Therefore our World-Honored One, true compassion aching, plucking out his own heart and gouging out his own entrails, finely examines the seven destinies, distinguishing by feelings and imaginings the many differences of inner and outer, more and less; and in detail discriminates the aggregate-demons, using false views to reveal the unevenness of shallow and deep in the contemplation of mind. The reason is this: he simply wishes us to ponder the suffering of the hells, arouse the bodhi-mind, and know that there is nirvāṇa, so that we no longer cling to the three realms. Alas, for us human beings! If one can grasp this vajra sword, the gate of the samādhi of the illusory, and cut the root of craving on the spot, then the empty flowers of the three realms vanish and the world sinks level; if one can pull out the thorn of views in a single instant, then the phantom film over the one mind wholly dissolves and empty space is shattered. It directly brings it about that not a mote remains, not a thought survives; one accomplishes the Buddha-fruit in this life and dissolves the outflows of habit from vast kalpas. This is what is meant by perfect bodhi returning to nothing attained. To believe and accept thus, to uphold and practice thus, is true diligence; it is named the true dharma-offering, and one may be called a heroic and mighty man, a being of great ease and sovereignty. What kindness would remain unrepaid? What virtue would remain unrequited? Otherwise one falls, and falls again — is that not painful?

The Dream-Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Scroll Forty-Two
Beating Time to the Wondrous Dharma Lotus Sutra
Master Hanshan
Recorded by his attendant Fushan; edited by his disciple Tongjiong; revised by the Lingnan disciple Liu Qixiang

It is because the World-Honored One appeared in the world solely for the sake of this one great cause and condition: namely, to open and show to all living beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which each and every one possesses from the beginning, and to cause them to awaken and enter it, so that they may attain present, actual realization. Only this one matter, and no other. To awaken to this knowledge and vision is to ascend the Buddha-ground; hence it is named the One Vehicle. Since the Tathāgata appeared in the world solely for this one great matter, the Dharma he taught is only the One Vehicle, with no other vehicle; and the teaching of his whole lifetime displays nothing but the principle, practice, cause, and fruit of the One Vehicle. Because during the first forty years the faculties were not yet ripe, what he set forth was only the principle and practice of the Three Vehicles; and because the revealed principle was not yet perfect, the practice was not true practice and the fruit was not true fruit. None of it was the ultimate Buddha-wisdom, but only a fostering and leading on, all expedient provisional arrangements, a gate for entering the Buddha’s wisdom. Yet though the words were expedient, the intent truly pointed to and returned to the One Vehicle, the ground of quiescence. It is like a finger pointing at the moon. Therefore he said: I now know that living beings have various desires, deeply clinging in their minds; according to their natures, by various causes, conditions, parables, phrases, and powers of expedient means, I teach them the Dharma — all of it so that they may attain the one Buddha Vehicle and the wisdom of all modes. Thus all that he spoke was for the One Vehicle. But those of inferior understanding took the words literally and clung to them, unable to grasp the purport beyond words. Therefore at the Perfection of Wisdom assemblies the Buddha winnowed them in many ways, and their faculties gradually ripened. So earlier, at the Laṅkāvatāra assembly, he taught the realm of noble wisdom self-awakened and apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness, in order to break the non-Buddhists’ views of deluded imagination and to remove the Small Vehicle’s clinging to names and phrases, directly revealing the ultimate One Vehicle, the true mark, the way beyond words. He wished directly to have living beings presently and suddenly realize the ground of the Buddhas’ self-awakened noble wisdom. Now, since they had already received the direct pointing that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is inherent in every person, and that this is the Buddhas’ self-awakened noble wisdom, the hearers could easily believe and easily enter; their faculties were ripe. Therefore at this Lotus assembly, in accordance with the preceding wisdom-realm, he directly revealed wondrous practice as the true cause, intending by this true cause to accord suddenly with the true fruit. Hence his very first words were that he had taught the Sutra of Innumerable Meanings and entered the samādhi of the abode of innumerable meanings. Now ‘innumerable meanings’ by no means denotes mere multiplicity; it displays this realm of the One Vehicle’s self-awakened noble wisdom, which transcends the measure of mind, intellect, and consciousness. Thus with the word-transcending wisdom he directly showed it to living beings, causing them to know it in silence and awaken and enter. One may say he first moved them by samādhi. Yet this wisdom-realm cannot be entered without the wondrous wisdom of the middle way; therefore he emitted the white-ray light between his brows, to show that the realm of faculties, dust, and consciousness in the daily life of living beings is precisely the Buddhas’ self-awakened noble wisdom. Hence the light illumined eighteen thousand lands. Birth and death and nirvāṇa are originally equal; therefore in the light the phenomena of the Dharma-realm, the beginning and end of living beings and Buddhas, appeared perfectly and were luminously clear to the eye. The intent was to reveal this true-mark mind-realm, which the Buddhas have realized and living beings have deluded; and now, wishing to cause living beings to realize it here and now, he pointed directly to what lies before them, not a hair’s breadth obscured. As for the four kinds of flowers raining from heaven and the six quakings of the earth, one may say the whole body was exposed and the very bottom overturned. His intent was that everyone should awaken without words and seize it on the spot. But because we have not departed from the mind-consciousness, our eyes remain dull and our heads confused; we cannot avoid discrimination and cannot truly believe. Because they discriminated by means of consciousness, Maitreya raised his doubt; and the reason he had to ask Mañjuśrī was to show that this wondrous realm of true mark cannot be realized without wisdom. When Mañjuśrī was questioned, he cited the original beginning of Lamp-Lighting Buddha to verify the auspicious signs of the present day. This was a subtle intonation and a side-communication; he had already pointed it out clearly and spoken it out. One may say he afterward pulled them up by wisdom. Yet, alas, because we have not forgotten our knowledge and vision, we still find it hard to comprehend the way beyond words, and words must again be used to guide us. Therefore all that involves speech is expedient. So the World-Honored One rose from samādhi and, having no alternative, again borrowed words to open them up. Then he plainly told them: the wisdom of the Buddhas is most profound and immeasurable, and the gate of that wisdom is hard to understand and hard to enter. Not only was all that was spoken during the past forty years the gate of wisdom; even today’s entering samādhi, emitting light, and manifesting auspicious signs is the gate of entering wisdom. Only this word-transcending way — only Buddhas with Buddhas can fully exhaust it; it is by no means reachable by the measuring and discriminating of mind-consciousness. Since it is called immeasurable, how could it be known by the measure of mind? In former times, indirect speech might still have left room for non-awakening; now that he directly reveals it, they are still blank and bewildered. Truly this gate of wisdom is hard to understand and enter. Why? Because all the immeasurable and boundless expedient parables, causes, conditions, and various phrases of former times were for the sake of displaying the One Vehicle, wishing to cause them ultimately to attain the Buddha-wisdom. Yet, alas, the hearers gave rise to understanding according to the words and in the end could not awaken and enter today’s matter. Since the time of his teaching was about to end and the hour of nirvāṇa had come, the situation allowed no stopping; so the Tathāgata exhausted his spiritual powers and greatly unfolded it, wishing directly that living beings might clearly see their own minds, understand the true mark, see the original dharmakāya, each realize it for himself, utterly abandon the clinging to words, and reach the ultimate place beyond words of self-awakened noble wisdom. Thus it begins with one light shining eastward, revealing the true mechanism of the Dharma-realm, and ends with the accomplishment of the four dharmas, realizing Samantabhadra’s eternal virtue. Seen in this light, the whole sutra of twenty-eight chapters is throughout an unfolding of the four words ‘opening, showing, awakening, entering’ the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and all that is set forth is nothing but the realm within that light. Beyond this, what remaining dharma is there? The reason is this: living beings are originally the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; yet, alas, they possess it and do not know it, have it before their eyes and do not see it. Now, if one would return from the false to the true, one must first awaken to the originally wondrous luminous mind. Therefore the principle-realm is shown first; then, in dependence on principle, practice is aroused, and the delusions of dust-like ignorance are purified and governed; only then can one realize and enter. Yet this true principle cannot be illumined without wisdom, and so Mañjuśrī’s great wisdom begins it; and it cannot be realized without practice, and so Samantabhadra’s wondrous practice completes it. Hence the first twenty-two chapters all display the perfect principle of the One Vehicle, the intent being to make this perfect principle the true cause; and the last six chapters all display the wondrous practice of the One Vehicle, the intent being to arouse wondrous practice in dependence on the perfect principle and to accomplish wondrous virtue through wondrous practice, so that wisdom and practice secretly merge and principle and wisdom are one suchness, and only then is the wondrous fruit realized. Therefore the four practices of Samantabhadra bring it to completion. It is what is meant by: nothing does not flow forth from this Dharma-realm; nothing does not return to this Dharma-realm. Thus the Avataṃsaka takes faith, understanding, practice, and realization as the foundation of Buddhahood, while this sutra takes opening, showing, awakening, and entering as the root of Buddhahood. Through the words of expedient teaching, one is opened and shown, and faith is aroused; from faith, understanding is aroused; in dependence on understanding, practice is aroused; and when practice is accomplished, understanding is cut off, and only then can one realize and enter. The two sutras are one from beginning to end, and their intents truly accord. Seen in this light, the passages that display the principle are all the purport of faith and understanding.

Now the display of the principle comprises twenty-two chapters. The Introduction chapter gives a general display of the true mechanism of the Dharma-realm, causing one to open, awaken, and enter it. The nine chapters from Expedient Means through Dharma Teacher, though described as teaching in three cycles and bestowing predictions on the three grades, are in fact especially a great opening of the equal Buddha-wisdom of all living beings. Because this Buddha-wisdom is complete in each and every one, without deficiency or remainder, whoever can know it realizes it at once. Hence it is said: of all who hear the Dharma, not one fails to become a Buddha; and whoever teaches this Dharma to others is a great Dharma Teacher. The intent is to show that this matter, though complete in everyone, is like a high plain: whoever digs will find water. This, however, is only the inherent Buddha-nature; one must rely on the conditional cause for it to become manifest, and the Dharma Teacher is that conditional cause. If one can make the mind accord with the Buddha’s mind and the practice accord with the Buddha’s practice — what is meant by entering the Tathāgata’s chamber, wearing the Tathāgata’s robe, and sitting on the Tathāgata’s seat — then one who can believe, understand, uphold, and maintain such dharmas is himself a Dharma Teacher. Therefore it says: follow and learn from such a teacher, and you shall see Buddhas as numerous as the Ganges’ sands. Thus within cause after cause the life of wisdom is unbroken, and one may look forward to final, actual realization. As for the various parables, causes, and conditions, all are meant to reveal this permanently abiding Buddha-nature, the supreme truth, the wonder of the one mind — all of it the realm within the light, a matter of our daily use. Hence whoever can believe this Dharma at once enters the Dharma-position; and so even one who holds a single verse or a single phrase, or has a single thought of sympathetic joy, is also given by me the prediction of bodhi. Thus each and every one is predicted to become a Buddha. This, however, is only through the opening and enlightening of expedient means, causing faith to arise; it is not realization and entry through understanding and practice. Therefore they are merely given predictions. Yet though predictions are given, many kalpas still intervene, because in principle one awakens suddenly and the traces vanish along with the awakening, while in fact they are not suddenly removed but exhausted by stages through gradual cultivation. This is what is meant by sudden awakening and gradual cultivation. When a single thought suddenly awakens to one’s own mind as not two with the Buddha, that is named seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha. Yet there remain beginningless, kalpa-spanning, dust-like afflictions and ignorance that cannot be suddenly purified; one must pass through many kalpas before reaching the ultimate. If one can, in the present single thought, suddenly cut off beginningless ignorance, that is named passing through many kalpas — what is meant by viewing that distant time as though it were today. Within this Dharma, when a single thought does not arise, the three periods are suddenly cut off; past and present are one period, and ordinary being and sage are level. Therefore the ten chapters of sutra text before the Dharma Teacher are all a great opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision in living beings.

Yet because they were merely opened and enlightened by words, the hearers only believed the words; they could not clearly see the wonder of their own minds. Whatever understanding they gained was but the trace of responsive transformation, not the realm of seeing the dharmakāya. This is what is meant by still standing outside the gate, lodging only in a thatched hut, forever stalled in the provisional trace. Therefore the sutra must proclaim and reveal the true realm of the dharmakāya's actual reward, causing them to see at once the wonder of their own minds; only then is it actual realization. Thus the Chapter of the Appearing Treasure-Stūpa suddenly reveals the mind itself, displaying the image of the dharmakāya. This is what is meant by opening the gate of expedient means and showing the mark of reality, wishing to cause living beings to know and see this true realm of the mark of reality. If we but shatter ignorance and at once open the ground of mind, then this body and mind of the five aggregates reveal the true dharmakāya Buddha; hence the seven-jeweled wondrous stūpa wells up before us, five hundred yojanas high. This true-mark wondrous dharma is what the dharmakāya expounds, teaching without teaching; therefore a great sound issues from within the stūpa. Because it wondrously accords with the dharmakāya, Prabhūtaratna gives his seal of confirmation. Its source is fundamentally without abiding; therefore the stūpa rests in empty space. Hearing what cannot be heard, they marvel that such a thing has never been. Because this Buddha-nature abides forever and is not extinguished, the Tathāgata's whole body is within the stūpa. Because its substance is the unborn, wherever this sutra is taught it is at once actually realized. Because pure wisdom is wondrous and perfect, the white-ray light illumines the ten directions. Because this wisdom-nature is inherent in everyone, lacking in none, the emanated Buddhas are each touched by the light. Because mind after mind is quiescent, all the worlds of the ten directions are thoroughly illumined as the site of quiescence. Because dharma after dharma is true, the three transformations of eight hundred myriad koṭis of lands become one Buddha-land of purity. Reaching this, roots and objects both perish and good and evil are equally erased; hence the three evil paths are suddenly empty and gods and humans are no longer seen. The Ganges-sands of nature-virtue are complete from the beginning; principal and dependent interpenetrate, self and other without obstruction. Hence the emanated Buddhas of the ten directions all gather within it. Yet though it is thus, they are still midway, because the view of arising and ceasing is not yet forgotten and the mind of grasping and rejecting is not yet erased. This is why they wish to see Prabhūtaratna but cannot yet see him. This is precisely what the ancient worthies meant by saying that even if one reaches the point where the cold pool holds the bright moon and the still night holds the bell's sound, losing nothing however it is struck, not scattering however the waves run, it is still a matter on the shore of birth and death. Why? Because the dark barrier of birth and death has not yet burst open. One must use non-abiding wisdom to develop it in accordance with the nature of awakening. This is why Śākyamuni, dwelling in empty space, opens the door of the seven-jeweled stūpa with his right hand. It directly causes beginningless ignorance to be shattered at a single thought; with one shout, empty space is pulverized; like a key turning in a lock, the great city gate opens. Thus the originally inherent dharmakāya appears at a single thought. Therefore Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata's whole body remains undispersed, as though entered into dhyāna; and because response and the way meet, he comes here to hear this sutra. Because the mind of arising and ceasing has perished and the real and the responsive are not two, Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna share one seat. This causal condition alone is inherent in everyone, lacking in none; hence the great assembly wished to see Prabhūtaratna. Yet because birth is fundamentally unborn and cannot be reached by conceptual consciousness, the Buddha's seat is high and distant; and because he abides in fundamental non-abiding, he lifts the whole assembly into empty space. This is the intrinsic virtue of living beings, and so it is directly shown in this way, that they may all know and see it and realize it without doubt. Thus the Tathāgata's fundamental intent is already revealed and the work of benefiting beings is complete. Yet though it is thus, it is Buddha-work in a flower of the sky, a bodhi-site in the moon's reflection — how could it be real dharma? Therefore he at once proclaims: the Tathāgata will before long enter nirvāṇa, wishing this dharma to abide forever and be honored alike through all ages. His intent is to gain the right person, so that the life of wisdom may be endless and inexhaustible. Hence it says: the Buddha wishes to entrust this wondrous dharma to one who exists. Seen in this light, the single chapter of the Appearing Treasure-Stūpa directly reveals the Buddha's knowledge and vision as it functions in the daily life of all living beings.

Yet this most profound and wondrous dharma is the realm the Buddhas themselves have realized, the supreme and foremost secret treasury — what is meant by the Buddhas' wisdom being most profound and immeasurable, and the gate of that wisdom hard to understand and hard to enter. Therefore the verses extensively praise this sutra as foremost of all; whoever upholds it attains the Buddha-way and is a true disciple of the Buddha, and one who can understand its meaning becomes the eye for gods and humans, let alone one who actually realizes it. Thus from faith, understanding is aroused, and through the opening and showing one awakens to this mind. Hence the five chapters that follow, from Devadatta through the Tathāgata's Measure of Life, are all images of awakening to one's own mind. Now this dharma has already been revealed and is inherent in everyone, lacking in none; yet because one has been deluded for so long, with deep roots of affliction and the tangles of self and dharma, sudden awakening is hard; one must borrow causes and conditions to awaken, seeking and then attaining. Thus the Devadatta chapter shows that awakening is neither easy nor hard, neither foolish nor wise: even the Tathāgata's great wisdom came only from many kalpas of diligent hardship, which is the difficulty of awakening; yet the nāga girl of eight years realized it at once, which is how very easy it is. The intent is to show that the seeker toils in vain through many kalpas while the one who lets go of mind awakens in an instant; it is only the power of a single thought's turning within the ocean of birth and death. When attachment to dharma and to love is forgotten and discriminating thoughts cease, one naturally awakens and at once attains non-retrogression. Hence the nāga girl, at the moment she offered her pearl, went at once to the Stainless World in the south, sat upon a jeweled lotus, and attained perfect enlightenment. But if thoughts of hate and love are not yet forgotten and the mind of grasping and rejecting is not yet erased, then attachment to dharma is not exhausted and the view of self is not dissolved; therefore one cannot awaken to pure perfect enlightenment. Hence even Śāriputra, for all his wisdom, could not avoid doubt. Thus the Chapter on Upholding the Sutra is taught, to show that the Small Vehicle is unequal to upholding this dharma and finds it hard to enter the world to benefit beings; what is needed is a superior faculty and sharp wisdom, vast compassion, the ability to do what is hard to do and endure what is hard to endure, wondrous accord with the unborn, and understanding without words. Only then is one fit to enter the world. Hence the Tathāgata silently regarded the eighty myriads of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas — precisely to stir the lesser capacity and enlarge the great vision. And these bodhisattvas, at once according with the Buddha-mind, roared the lion's roar and vowed to go back and forth through the worlds of the ten directions, cultivating in accord with dharma, enduring every kind of austerity; and they said: the Buddha himself knows our minds. This is what is meant by teacher and disciple perfectly attuned, water and milk merging — the right person has been found. Yet though there be one fit to bear it, if the method is not found, one still cannot awaken. Because the roots of affliction are deep and hardest to tame, the Four Practices of Ease are taught to show the method of awakening. The intent is that one who awakens to this dharma should first honor the pure nature-precepts of the three karmas; one must accord the mind with the Buddha-mind, and with great compassion as foremost, must enter the Tathāgata's chamber; one's practice must accord with the Buddha's practice, and with patience as foremost, must wear the Tathāgata's robe; since the Buddha-wisdom is like space, depending on nothing, one must abide where the Buddha abides, resting in the emptiness of dharmas, and must sit upon the Tathāgata's seat. Only then can one suddenly awaken to this dharma, so that entering the world holds no difficulty and afflictions are easily broken — like winning a battle and receiving the topknot-pearl as reward. One must have faith in one's own mind, investigate and awaken for oneself, and only then is one fit to inherit the Buddha's family style. Hence the Chapter on Emerging from the Earth shows the image of the mind's own unfolding. What enters through a gate is not the family treasure; only what flows out from one's own breast covers heaven and earth. Therefore even the bodhisattvas who came from other lands, though bodhisattvas, were still not equal to the task; hence the words: I do not need you to protect this sutra; I have my own sixty thousand Ganges-sands of followers. At that moment the great trichiliocosm quaked and split, and countless bodhisattvas surged forth at once. Only this Ganges-sands nature-virtue, complete from the beginning, lies at the gates of each person's six faculties, emitting light and shaking the earth, never lacking in function. Hence the sixty thousand Ganges-sands of followers, their bodies bearing immeasurable radiance. Because roots and dust share one source and bondage and liberation are not two, they were all beneath this world; because the middle has no substance, like intertwined reeds, they are said to dwell in empty space. Because present afflictions all flow from the dharma-nature, they are said to be those formerly taught. Because every thing is true and every particular wondrous, the great assembly are all leaders of the chanting. Because one practice wholly contains all practices and one dharma wholly contains all dharmas, each one has many followers. Because all they do is dedicated to the dharmakāya, each proceeded to empty space to behold the two Buddhas Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni and bow their heads at their feet. Because they wondrously accord with the Buddha-mind, they inquired of the World-Honored One with various consolations, and the World-Honored One confirmed them. Only thus can one hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom. This is a matter on the side of the dharmakāya, not reachable by conceptual consciousness. Hence Maitreya and the eight thousand Ganges-sands of great beings all gave rise to doubt; and the Tathāgata at this point greatly opened the secret and directly revealed the original, ever-abiding ground of mind. Hence he says: the Tathāgata now wishes to proclaim and expound the wisdom of the Buddhas, the power of the Buddhas' sovereign spiritual penetrations, and the power of the Buddhas' lion-striding. Thus the Chapter on the Measure of Life is taught, to show the measure of the dharmakāya's life and exhaust the fundamental intent, revealing the wondrous luminous ever-abiding true mind: unmoving yet all-pervading, filling the ten directions, responding universally according to conditions, transforming wondrously without fixed direction, long or short according to conditions, hidden or manifest without obstruction. This clarifies that the Tathāgata's wisdom is most profound and immeasurable, and that through various skillful means he manifests to benefit beings, showing the meaning that the gate of his wisdom is hard to understand and hard to enter. He also says: I dwell on Vulture Peak, ever present and undestroyed; though the great fire burns, this land is peaceful — revealing the true realm of the mark of reality. If this were not the Buddha's knowledge and vision, how could one know and see it? This Buddha's true power of knowledge and vision, the realm of self-enlightened noble wisdom, is why the three vehicles throughout the world cannot fathom it with the measuring mind. So it is. Thus the five chapters — Devadatta; Upholding the Sutra; the Practices of Ease; Emerging from the Earth; and the Tathāgata's Measure of Life — all cause living beings to awaken to the Buddha's knowledge and vision. This is clear. As for the Chapter on Distinguishing Merits, it supremely reveals the supreme benefit of wondrously awakening to the non-action of one's own mind. That the merit of upholding the sutra surpasses jewel-offerings to buddha-lands stirs the Small Vehicle to aspire to the Great. That many kalpas of practicing the five pāramitās do not equal the merit of hearing the Tathāgata's Measure of Life urges provisional-teaching bodhisattvas to abandon the provisional and realize the true. That the merit of a single thought of sympathetic joy brings inconceivable reward shows that this dharma is entered through faith. That the crime of a single thought of slander is inexhaustible through kalpas is what is meant by the crime of unbelief being above all crimes; this encourages icchantikas and non-Buddhists to arouse great-vehicle right faith. That the reward of cultivation is immeasurable is meant to let ordinary beings accomplish it in one lifetime, free of the fear of the Buddha-way's long duration. That one who diligently upholds and circulates this sutra gains the merit of pure six faculties reveals a sample of present realization and shows that diligent upholding surpasses even a single thought of sympathetic joy. As for Never-Disparaging, one may say he awakened to the equality of true suchness and deeply attained it himself; hence, using the seed of Buddha-nature, he universally regarded the four assemblies and bestowed predictions. Reaching this, discrimination is forgotten and right and wrong come to an end; one may call it the utmost of wondrous awakening. Only thus can one bear the great matter. Hence the Chapter on Spiritual Powers is taught, to reveal the image of the inconceivable merit of awakening the mind. The assembly from the earth now vows to uphold the sutra, and the Tathāgata exhausts his spiritual powers and greatly unfolds them, revealing that the merit of awakening the mind is vast and inconceivable. If we can reach this thorough awakening to the mind-only realm, then no single thing is not Buddha-dharma; hence the Tathāgata, before the great assembly, manifests great spiritual power, extending his broad, long tongue up to the Brahma heaven. No single form is not the Buddha-body; hence from every pore of his body he emits countless colored lights, illumining the bodies of all Buddhas in the ten directions. At this state, principal and dependent interpenetrate and self and other are not two. As it is said, in the boundless ocean of lands, self and other are not separated by the tip of a hair; hence the Buddhas of the ten directions likewise emit immeasurable light. Throughout the ten ages past and present, beginning and end never depart from the present thought; hence the Buddhas also manifest spiritual power for a full hundred thousand years. When I press my finger, the ocean-seal emits light; coughing, spitting, moving an arm — all merge with the true reality; hence the sounds of clearing the throat and snapping the fingers reach all worlds in the ten directions. Reaching this, all living beings realize perfect enlightenment and the sentient and insentient alike accomplish the Buddha-way; hence in those ten directions the eight kinds of beings, gods and humans, all see the Buddha from afar, teaching this Wondrous Dharma Lotus Sutra. If one can awaken to one's own mind, then the very implements of affliction become the true cause of Buddhahood; hence the adornments they remove all become jeweled canopies, covering all the Buddhas here. Mind and realm are vast and clear, limits dissolve and are forgotten; hence the lands of the ten directions are penetrated without obstruction, as one Buddha-land. Yet the supremely vast spiritual power of our Buddha, exhausting the bounds of living beings — were he to use it to display the merit of wondrous awakening, through immeasurable kalpas it still could not be exhausted, revealing that self-enlightened noble wisdom is by no means a realm of consciousness. All the dharmas the Tathāgata possesses, all his sovereign spiritual powers, all his secret treasuries, all his profound matters, are proclaimed and revealed in this sutra. Hence he supremely declares that all conditioned, adorned merit is in no way equal to the supreme merit of upholding this sutra. In praising so greatly the supremacy of upholding the sutra, though the words reveal the supremacy of the dharma, the real intent is to arouse in the Small Vehicle the mind that delights in the Great, desiring that everyone realize the mind-source to the utmost before being fit to bear the great dharma. Hence it says: such a person has no doubt whatever concerning the Buddha-way. Therefore the Chapter on Entrustment is taught next, concluding the Tathāgata's fundamental intent in appearing in the world and teaching the dharma. The World-Honored One rose from his seat and with his right hand stroked the crowns of the immeasurable bodhisattvas who had emerged from the earth, consoling and entrusting them: for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas I have cultivated this hard-won dharma of supreme perfect enlightenment; now I entrust it to you. You should single-mindedly circulate this dharma, spreading it widely so that it increases. Three times he stroked the crowns of the bodhisattvas, entrusting them to uphold and widely proclaim this dharma, so that all living beings may hear and know it. For all living beings each inherently possess the Buddha's wisdom, the Tathāgata's wisdom, natural wisdom, and have been deluded and unaware of it; now the Tathāgata in this sutra fully reveals it without any secret stinginess — the Tathāgata is the great almsgiver to all living beings. And he says: in future ages, if there is one person who can believe the Tathāgata's wisdom, one should expound this sutra so that he may hear and know it, in order that he may attain the Buddha-wisdom. If one can benefit beings by such skillful means, one may be said to repay the Buddha's deep kindness. Because the Tathāgata's repeated admonitions were earnest and the bodhisattvas' resolve to uphold was sincere, the bodhisattvas each rejoiced and increased their reverence, and three times all proclaimed: as the World-Honored One has said, we shall reverently carry it out; may you have no concern. Thus the Tathāgata's appearance in the world was fundamentally to open and show to living beings the Buddha's knowledge and vision and cause them to awaken and enter. Now, through layer upon layer of revelation, he has reached the point beyond words, and the listeners' mind of understanding has also become thoroughly clear; the living beings' mind of understanding has reached its utmost and the Tathāgata's work is complete. As for setting out on practice and cultivation, that depends on each person's own assent; hence he causes the Buddhas of the ten directions each to return to their own lands and abide each in peace. Since practice and realization are not yet complete, the stūpa of Many Jewels Buddha is left to remain as before. These twenty-two chapters all aim at the gate of opening, showing, awakening, and entering, to accomplish the resources of faith and understanding; the six chapters that follow all accomplish virtue through practice. This is what is meant by first relying on the perfect principle to arouse perfect practice, and then relying on perfect practice to realize the perfect principle; understanding and practice mutually support each other, and only then is the fruit of the ultimate attained, revealing the utmost of entering the Buddha's knowledge and vision.

The six chapters from the Former Deeds of the Bodhisattva Medicine King through Samantabhadra's Encouragement all clarify how practice accomplishes virtue, displaying the image of entering the Buddha's knowledge and vision. Now, at the outset of arousing practice, Medicine King must be the one to unfold it, because the medicine of contemplative wisdom cures the sickness of affliction; when wisdom arises, delusion perishes, and at a single thought one is transformed into supreme awareness, attaining great sovereignty — hence he is named Medicine King. The reason living beings are not sovereign is that the two attachments of self and dharma obstruct them. These two attachments are of two kinds: the discriminated and the innate. Now, having awakened to the wondrous mind, by the power of calm abiding and insight that is none other than mind, one purely breaks the two obstructions of discriminated self and dharma and ascends the first ground. Hence Medicine King burning his body is the image of breaking the attachment to self; Joyful Vision burning his arms is the image of breaking the attachment to dharma. To break the two obstructions, pure wisdom is indispensable; hence the Buddha he served is named Pure Light of Sun and Moon Virtue. Awakening to the inherently possessed dharmakāya and realizing the equal true suchness, he attained the samādhi that manifests all physical forms — the image from the first ground through the seventh. By the inner perfuming of this true suchness he took fragrant oils; by at once abandoning the storehouse consciousness his light illumined eighty myriad koṭis of Ganges-sands of worlds, and the Buddhas therein praised him as one — only this is named true diligence, named the true dharma-offering. When the first seven turning consciousnesses had thus dissolved, roots and dust were both extinguished; hence his body burned for twelve hundred years. Thereupon he entered the position of true dharma, not apart from the Buddha's family; hence he was reborn in the land of the Buddha Pure Light of Sun and Moon Virtue, and because of the constant light shining there it is said that that Buddha is even now present — the image of entering the eighth ground. Yet though he had reached this and broken the innate attachment to self, the innate attachment to dharma remained unforgotten and the view of the dharmakāya was not yet dissolved; hence he declared that the World-Honored One was still in the world, because the dharmakāya does not permit seeing one another in succession. Yunmen said: even if you penetrate through and reach the very edge of the dharmakāya, if the dharma-attachment is unforgotten and self-view still remains, the light is still not fully transparent. This too must be dissolved; hence the original Buddha entered nirvāṇa in the latter part of the night, and the Bodhisattva Joyful Vision at once gave up both arms — the image of partially breaking the innate attachment to dharma. It is what is said: the two obstructions of discrimination are transcended at the stage of Extreme Joy, while the innate attachment to dharma is removed ground by ground. Because only the attachment is broken and not the dharma itself, the two arms were restored as before. All this relies on the power of the Lotus Sutra's samādhi of the mark of reality; hence it extensively praises the merit of this sutra — its true and wondrous benefit. Whoever cultivates it gains benefit without exception, like the cold finding fire, the naked finding clothes, the sick finding a physician.

If the power of calm abiding and insight of this Lotus samādhi advances deeply without cease, then emerging from the eighth ground one reaches the ninth and tenth and dwells in the position of Dharma Teacher, teaching the dharma and benefiting beings, responding wondrously without fixed direction — what is called the pure wondrous dharmakāya, serenely answering all. Hence the Chapter on the Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound is taught, to demonstrate the actual realization of the samādhi that manifests all physical forms; it shows the image of wondrous practice issuing from the real and entering the conventional. Question: when this chapter was taught, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted the light of the mark of the great being, the uṣṇīṣa light, and also emitted the white-ray light between his brows, illumining eastward through a hundred and eight myriads of koṭis of nayutas of Ganges-sands of Buddha-worlds; and beyond that number there was a world named Adorned with Pure Light, whose land had a Buddha named Pure Flower Constellation-King Wisdom. What does this mean? Answer: this cites the fruit to verify the image of the One Vehicle's true cause. According to the Laṅkāvatāra, after teaching the Tathāgata's supreme One Vehicle Chan it says: if śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can remove all habitual faults and awaken to the selflessness of dharmas, then they emerge from the intoxication of samādhi and awaken within the unconditioned realm; having awakened, they again enter the supramundane, supreme-of-supreme unconditioned realm, fulfill all requisites, and shall attain the Tathāgata's inconceivable and sovereign dharmakāya. This dharmakāya is the mind-made body. It also says there are three kinds of mind-made body. First, the mind-made body of the bliss of samādhi: from the first ground through the eighth, exhausting the limit of true suchness, having abandoned the storehouse consciousness and cut off the innate attachment to self, one dwells in the ocean of mind so that the waves of consciousness no longer arise; one's own mind is still, dwelling in the bliss of samādhi, knowing that the appearances of one's own mind and their objects have no nature. The earlier Joyful Vision is thus the image of dwelling in the bliss-of-samādhi mind-made body; and that samādhi manifesting all physical forms is the image of comprehending the mind-only realm, realizing the mind-made body of the bliss of samādhi — yet that can only receive the bliss within samādhi, and so cannot manifest all bodies. Second, the mind-made body of the nature of the nature of awakening to dharmas: from the eighth ground one observes and awakens to dharmas such as the illusory as all nonexistent, and body and mind attain the samādhi of the illusory and the remaining samādhi-gates, with immeasurable marks and sovereign powers, bright as a wondrous flower's adornment, swift as thought, like a dream, an illusion, a water-moon, a mirror-image — not made yet as if made, as if made; all forms and their various limbs are fully adorned; one enters all Buddha-lands and great assemblies, penetrating the dharma of self-nature. This is named the mind-made body of the nature of the nature of awakening to dharmas. Third, the mind-made body of the class-born, non-acting: awakening to all Buddha-dharmas as conditions, one naturally attains the mark of bliss — this is named the class-born, non-acting mind-made body. Seen in this light, the Chapter on the Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound shows the image of the second, the mind-made body of the nature of the nature of awakening to dharmas. As for the white ray between the brows, it represents the wondrous wisdom of the middle way, the image of the causal mind; the uṣṇīṣa on the crown is the mark of the invisible summit, the image of the unsurpassed fruit of awakening. Because the bodhisattva of the eighth ground realizes the one mind's true suchness and advances to the ninth, issuing the function of true suchness and attaining the samādhi of the illusory, manifesting bodies and teaching the dharma and dwelling in the position of Dharma Teacher, he is named Wondrous Sound. Because the true causal mind accords with the fruit of awakening, the two lights of uṣṇīṣa and white ray are emitted together. Because he enters the supramundane, supreme-of-supreme unconditioned realm, the light illumines eastward through a hundred and eight myriads of koṭis of nayutas of Ganges-sands of Buddha-worlds. Because dharma and reward are realized together, the land is named Adorned with Pure Light. Because the pure true cause wondrously accords with the fruit-substance, that land has a Buddha named Pure Flower Constellation-King Wisdom. When cause and fruit secretly meet, one can with a single sound expound immeasurable dharmas and attain the ten inexhaustible phrases; hence the bodhisattvas of that land are named Wondrous Sound. In this position one attains the samādhi of the illusory and the remaining samādhi-gates; hence the samādhi of the mark of the wondrous banner and so forth, a hundred thousand myriad koṭis of Ganges-sands of great samādhis. Because the fruit-ground awakening is the root causal mind, Śākyamuni Buddha's light shines upon his body. Because the bodhisattva of this position can recall his original vow and enter all Buddha-lands and assemblies, transforming and penetrating the virtue of self-nature, he vows to go to the Sahā world to see Śākyamuni Buddha and the bodhisattvas. Because the bodhisattva of this ground can manifest immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers, swift as thought like the adornment of a wondrous flower, without rising from his seat or stirring his body, by the power of samādhi he first conjures before his seat eighty-four thousand jeweled lotus flowers. This bodhisattva manifests a body though not a body, like a dream, an illusion, a water-moon, a mirror-image, not made yet as if made, as if made; all forms and their various limbs are fully adorned. Hence his eyes are like the broad leaves of the blue lotus; even if a hundred thousand myriad moons were joined together his face would be more upright than that; his body is true gold, adorned with immeasurable virtues, his majesty blazing and his radiance shining, all marks complete, like Nārāyaṇa's firm body. Because the bodhisattva of this ground can contain and receive all the dharma-clouds and dharma-rains of the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Buddha he served is named Cloud-Thunder-Sound King. Because root and dust, every particle, pervade the Dharma-realm and fully possess dharma-bliss, universally amid toil manifesting according to faculties, for twelve thousand years, with ten myriad musical performances and eighty-four thousand seven-jeweled bowls offered, he could serve the Buddhas of the ten directions and purify Buddha-lands; hence he drew near and made offerings to many Buddhas. Without moving from the fundamental limit he performs the work of saving beings; hence he manifests various bodies and everywhere teaches this sutra to living beings. This precisely corresponds to the ninth and tenth grounds and to the image of Equal Enlightenment. To show living beings the image of present realization in daily use, those who came with him, eighty-four thousand in number, all attained the samādhi manifesting all physical forms, and the immeasurable bodhisattvas of this Sahā world likewise attained this samādhi and dhāraṇī. Because function does not depart from substance, he returned to his native land and, encircling the Buddha, addressed him. Yet this wondrous function of spiritual power lies only between the four elements, roots, and dust — the power of body-and-mind transformation; hence forty thousand and twenty-two thousand gods all attained the patient acceptance of the unborn. This is precisely the image of the mind-made body of the nature of the nature of awakening to dharmas. Because of entering and emerging from samādhi there is the mark of coming and going; as for Avalokiteśvara's universal manifestation, equally contemplating and universally illumining, there is no trace of coming or going here or there — so Avalokiteśvara's wondrous response shows the image of the various class-born, non-acting mind-made bodies. Yet this mind-made body, from Equal Enlightenment entering the ocean of the wondrous-enlightenment fruit, has already attained the noble wisdom self-awakened by all Buddhas and its supreme bliss, deeply entering the ocean of wondrous adornment, flowing against the stream to manifest bodies throughout the ten realms, responding without thought — what is called the adornment of wondrous marks, the holy class-body, appearing all at once like a mind-made body-land, self and other without obstruction or hindrance; hence it is called the class-born, non-acting mind-made body. This is the equal manifestation of the great perfect mirror-wisdom after entering wondrous enlightenment; hence it is named the power of universally manifesting spiritual transformation. Because the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, by the power of the vajra samādhi of illusory hearing, perfuming, and cultivation, has extinguished arising and ceasing so that quiescence appears before him and he suddenly transcends the world and the supramundane, he attains above the same power of compassion as the Buddhas of the ten directions and below the same grieving aspiration as the beings of the six paths; thus with one body he universally responds to all. Hence the thirty-two responses, the four inconceivables, the fourteen fearlessnesses, the nineteen kinds of teaching, the eight difficulties and two requests — none fails to receive response. This is the success of the perfect cultivation of the Lotus samādhi of wondrous practice, its wonder reaching its utmost here. Silently comprehending the holy purport, one may say: principle reaches its limit and feeling is forgotten; how could any simile match it? At the end, two night-moons; effortlessly they fall into the stream before. Truly this dharma is most profound and subtle, and few are able to believe it; only those who have deeply cultivated and attained it themselves believe it without doubt. Seen in this light, when this wondrous practice is complete and one thereby accords with the Buddha-mind, three kinds of empowerment are felt, guarding against fault and removing transgression, so that the practitioner's outer demons do not disturb him and inner habits leave no remainder; only then can he attain the two turnings-about and fully perfect the wondrous fruit. Therefore the last three chapters are taught to conclude the assembly. The three kinds of empowerment are empowerment by spiritual power, empowerment by dharma-power, and empowerment by manifesting body, face, and speech. In order, the last three chapters correspond to the three empowerments; thus the Dhāraṇī chapter is the image of empowerment by spiritual power. The Laṅkāvatāra speaks of two kinds of empowerment: manifesting body, face, and speech, and the spiritual power of hand-consecration; because this sutra proceeds by opening, showing, awakening, and entering, dharma-power is needed. The Sanskrit dhāraṇī is rendered here as total retention: retaining all dharmas and holding immeasurable meanings — another name for the one mind. Calling it a divine mantra means it is the secret true-mark mind-seal of all Buddhas, like the great general's tally of authority in the world. A practitioner of superior faculty and sharp wisdom can leap straight in at once; yet beginningless habit-energy is subtle, hidden, and deeply buried, and though ground down by the power of calm abiding and insight, there are things so deep, firm, and remote that the power of wisdom cannot reach them. If one does not rely on the secret mind-seal and mantra-wheel of the Tathāgatas to attack them, then once inner habit erupts outer demons easily invade, and how could one escape birth and death, realize the true and eternal, and enter the Land of Quiescent Light? Hence no practitioner attains accomplishment without relying on the secret divine mantra. Practice has exoteric and esoteric aspects: the power of the former right contemplation is the exoteric practice, while this dhāraṇī is the esoteric practice. The Śūraṃgama says: if a practitioner's habit-energy is not yet removed, he should single-mindedly recite my secret divine mantra of the Sitatapatra Uṣṇīṣa. This is why, when the wondrous practice of the Lotus samādhi was complete, the World-Honored One, grieving for the Dharma-ending age, again taught this Dhāraṇī chapter to deeply guard against error and delusion; this is what is meant by empowerment by spiritual power. The Śūraṃgama says: the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, through this mantra-mind, attain supreme perfect enlightenment. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, holding this mantra-mind, subdue all demons and control all non-Buddhists. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, riding this mantra-mind, sit on jeweled lotuses and appear in dust-mote lands. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, containing this mantra-mind, turn the great dharma-wheel in dust-mote lands. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, upholding this mantra-mind, can throughout the ten directions stroke heads and bestow predictions. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, relying on this mantra-mind, can throughout the ten directions rescue and relieve every suffering. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, following this mantra-mind, can throughout the ten directions serve good teachers and in the four deportments make offerings as they wish, becoming Dharma-princes in the assemblies of Ganges-sands of Tathāgatas. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, practicing this mantra-mind, can throughout the ten directions gather and receive kindred causes, causing the Small Vehicle no terror before the secret treasury. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, reciting this mantra-mind, attain supreme awakening, sit beneath the bodhi tree, and enter great nirvāṇa. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, transmitting this mantra-mind, entrust the Buddha-dharma after the Buddha's extinction, ultimately maintaining it, and all are purified in the strict purity of the precepts. It also says: you living beings who have not yet exhausted rebirth, who arouse a sincere mind to attain arhatship — if you do not hold this mantra while sitting in the place of awakening, there is no way for body and mind to keep far from demonic matters. Alas! Even the Buddhas are thus; how much more the beings of this Dharma-ending age, defiled by karma! Because this divine mantra is the mind-seal of every Buddha, it is said to have been spoken by Buddhas as numerous as sixty-two koṭis of Ganges-sands. That Medicine King speaks the mantra first is because this secret seal is the foremost of wondrous practices. Next Vaiśravaṇa speaks, because the heavenly kings are the four world-protecting kings and the lords of the realm of birth and death; Vaiśravaṇa is the heavenly king of the north. The northern trigram is Kan, and Kan means sinking — one yang sunk between two yin, showing the image of the perils of birth and death. Thus when a practitioner, amid the perils of birth and death, wishes to realize bodhi at once, without empowerment by spiritual power how could he rescue the multitudes from difficulty and bring them out of the perilous road? Next comes the world-protecting king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the heavenly king of the east. The eastern trigram is Zhen, and Zhen means movement; the east is the head of all movement. The Yi says: good and ill fortune, regret and remorse, arise from movement. The treatise says: movement must entail suffering. Thus when a practitioner, amid the movement and turmoil of birth and death, performs the practice of utmost stillness, without empowerment by spiritual power how could he reach the realm of quiescence? As for the southern trigram Li, Li means adherence, the image of empty brightness; the western trigram Dui, Dui means pleasure. In a realm of empty brightness and delight there is no need of empowerment; hence those two heavenly kings need not speak. What follows with the rākṣasī is because rākṣasas are dark, obscure ghosts, flying and eating human flesh, and the female is the very extreme of yin and evil. This shows the rākṣasī of ignorance, whose karmic habits slay the dharmakāya. Now, investigating and exhausting it through calm abiding and insight, one transforms ignorance into the wondrous luminous light of mind; hence the rākṣasī too vows by her own body to protect those who uphold, read, recite, and cultivate this sutra, at once causing the three poisons of ignorance to be utterly purified without remainder — what is meant by causing all poisonous drugs to be dissolved. Because one wondrously accords with the dharmakāya and secretly penetrates the Dharma-realm, incense-offering is foremost; because all afflictions should transform into supreme awareness, offerings of every kind of lamp are foremost. This is the purity of the six faculties and the perfect luminosity of the eight consciousnesses; hence sixty-eight thousand people all attained the patient acceptance of the unborn. All this is the benefit of empowerment by spiritual power. When empowerment by spiritual power has dispelled outer demons, if there were no inner perfuming by dharma-power, how could one purify inner obstructions and realize the two turnings-about? Therefore the chapter on the former deeds of King Wondrous Adornment is taught, to show the image of empowerment by dharma-power. The Laṅkāvatāra says: if one is not established by spiritual power, one falls into the deluded views of non-Buddhists and into the hopes of śrāvakas and multitudes of demons, and does not attain supreme bodhi. Hence from the first ground to the seventh, contemplation with marks predominates; if not empowered, one falls into the evil views of non-Buddhists. From the eighth ground up, contemplation without marks predominates; if not empowered, one falls into the ground of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles. At the ninth and tenth grounds and Equal Enlightenment, without empowerment one cannot enter the wondrous. Seen in this light, the preceding empowerment by the divine mantra is the image from the first to the seventh ground; hence it speaks only of keeping far from demonic matters. This present chapter is the image of the ninth ground and above entering the wondrous; hence it speaks of the two sons turning their father's evil mind and all going forth from home together — the image of the inherent awakening emerging from its entanglement. How is this made clear? King Wondrous Adornment is the image of the Tathāgatagarbha in entanglement; now, manifesting and issuing the original truth, it is called former deeds, because the Tathāgatagarbha is itself the wondrous adornment fruit-substance. Now, deluded, it becomes the ālaya-consciousness, named the mind-king of the eight consciousnesses; from this come the first six and seventh turning consciousnesses, creating all karma and receiving all suffering. If one turns the sixth consciousness into the wisdom of wondrous observation, the storehouse consciousness has no defilement to receive; hence he is named Pure Storehouse. If one turns the seventh consciousness into the wisdom of equality, the view of discrimination is dissolved and the seeing-part extinguished, and one attains clarity of the dharma-eye; hence he is named Pure Eye. This is the image of turning defilement into purity. Turning these two consciousnesses relies wholly on the power of calm abiding and insight; hence Lady Pure Virtue is the image of calm abiding and insight. The lady is the virtue of earth, the extreme of yielding compliance, with much power of inner aid; she is also the image of initial awakening. Through the inner support of calm abiding and insight, according with the nature of awakening and purifying ignorance, she is named Pure Virtue; hence the two sons she bore could turn their father king's evil mind. For this power of calm abiding and insight is the dharmakāya-bodhisattva's attainment of the undiscriminating mind, corresponding to the Buddhas' wisdom-function; relying only on dharma-power, he cultivates naturally, perfumes true suchness, and extinguishes ignorance. Hence the Buddha he served is named Cloud-Thunder-Sound Constellation-King Flower Wisdom, and his land is named Adorned with Pure Light. Through non-abiding wisdom purifying the substance of his own mind, the two sons rose into empty space, manifested various transformations, and turned their father's evil mind. Because the sixth and seventh are turned at the causal stage, the two sons first asked to go forth from home; and the seeds and habits within the storehouse consciousness, perfumed by the power of calm abiding and insight, were all turned from defilement to purity, so that the eighty-four thousand members of the king's inner palace all became capable of upholding the Wondrous Dharma Lotus Sutra. Now the reason the Tathāgatagarbha does not emerge from the bitter destinies of birth and death is that they are all created by the sixth consciousness and dragged along by the power of karma. Now that the sixth consciousness is turned, the cause of birth and death in the eighth consciousness is cut off. Because it was originally undefiled, the Bodhisattva Pure Storehouse had already, through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, penetrated the samādhi of separation from all evil — what is called the non-doer, non-maker, non-receiver, because fundamentally without nature, and because when initial awakening has merit the inherent awakening becomes manifest. The king attained the samādhi of the gathering of all Buddhas and could know the secret treasuries of the Buddhas. Because when the sixth and seventh are turned the fifth and eighth are turned at once, so that not one of the four elements, roots, and dust fails to be turned, he went with the king and his ministers and forty-two thousand people all at once to the Buddha's place. Because turning defilement into purity releases the entanglement, they removed the necklaces from their necks and scattered them before the Buddha. Because they wondrously accord with the dharmakāya and the eternal, blissful, self, and pure wondrous virtue of nirvāṇa, four kinds of jeweled terraces were conjured in empty space, and on the terraces a great jeweled couch spread with hundreds of thousands of myriads of celestial garments, upon which a Buddha sat cross-legged. For empty space's eternal oneness is the virtue of true permanence; the celestial garments fitting the body is the virtue of true bliss; the Buddha seated cross-legged is the virtue of true self; the emission of great light is the virtue of true purity. The images of the four virtues are plainly visible. Reaching this, the work of calm abiding and insight is complete and they emerge from entanglement together; hence the king, his lady, his two sons, and all the retinue went forth from home. This is reliance on dharma-power perfuming true suchness — the conditional Buddha-nature. Hence it says: our two sons, by spiritual transformations, turned our evil mind, causing us to dwell peacefully in the Buddha-dharma and see the Tathāgata. These two sons are our good teachers; wishing to arouse our past-life roots of goodness and benefit us, they came to be born in our house. These good teachers are a great cause and condition, guiding and transforming us so that we see the Buddha. All this displays the power of the perfuming of conditional causes. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: it is like smelting gold ore; the gold is not something that exists because of the smelting, yet though it was always gold, only by smelting is it accomplished. Once it becomes the substance of true gold, it is never again ore. Hence it says: from today I shall no longer follow my mind's impulses, nor give rise to evil minds of wrong view, arrogance, anger, and the like. All toil becomes pure at a single thought; hence at that time eighty-four thousand people, far from dust and free of defilement, attained purity of the dharma-eye amid all dharmas. Yet without inner perfuming by dharma-power, how could they have reached this? Hence this chapter is the image of empowerment by dharma-power; it is clear. Now when the practitioner relies on the empowerment of spiritual power so that outer demons do not disturb him, and is aided by the empowerment of dharma-power so that inner obstructions do not arise, then within and without are pure, body and mind are liberated, and the wondrous practice is complete; the true suchness he realizes is equal to the Dharma-realm. All this borrows the fruit-virtue as the power of the causal mind. When the causal mind is perfect the fruit-virtue is also full; hence the Chapter on Samantabhadra's Encouragement is taught to conclude the assembly.

The Chapter on Samantabhadra's Encouragement is empowerment by manifesting body, face, and speech, showing the image of entering the Buddha's knowledge and vision. Because one cultivates Samantabhadra's practice with a mind that matches the Dharma-realm, at the first arousal of the mind one relies on this as the true cause; hence one finally attains wondrous accord with the eternal fruit. Now Samantabhadra is of two kinds. First, Samantabhadra before the path, in the position of Equal Enlightenment: practice filling the Dharma-realm is called Pu (universal), and being adjacent to the ultimate and next to the sage is called Xian (worthy) — this is the causal position. Second, Samantabhadra after the path: matching the true Dharma-realm is called Pu, and encompassing the myriad transformations is called Xian — this is entering the ocean of the wondrous-enlightenment fruit, not dwelling in nirvāṇa, flowing against the stream and emerging; though dwelling in the fruit-position, he does not abandon the causal gate — this is the Samantabhadra of the present. Because at the first arousal of the mind one awakens to this substance and arouses practice in dependence on it, and when practice arises understanding is cut off, it is called encouragement to arouse. Now this Samantabhadra takes the Dharma-realm as his body, pervading the turmoil and deluded imaginings and toil of all living beings, becoming a companion in toil to all humans, gods, spirits, ghosts, and demonic retinues. Hence he comes from the east with immeasurable assemblies, each manifesting the power of spiritual transformation, to this Sahā world, to the place of Śākyamuni Buddha. Because the true limit of the dharmakāya is where mind-consciousness is transcended, he is said to be in the Buddha-land of the King of Supreme Virtue of Precious Majesty. This word-transcending way is now perfumed by dharma-power and penetrated through words and speech; hence it says he heard from afar that in this Sahā world the Lotus Sutra is being taught, and came with the great assembly to listen and receive it. It is what is meant by: though not relying on the path of words, one also does not cling to wordlessness. Hence it says: may the World-Honored One be pleased to teach it. Yet when Samantabhadra asked in this way, the World-Honored One added not a single word in reply, precisely revealing that the word-transcending way admits no sound — the very image of forgetting words and cutting off realization. So Samantabhadra immediately asked: after the Tathāgata's extinction, how can one obtain this sutra? Formerly the great bodhisattvas had only heard of reading, reciting, upholding, and maintaining it, but had never heard of anyone obtaining it; now that Samantabhadra asks about obtaining this sutra, it is enough to know that through the preceding understanding and practice one realizes and enters here. Thus it is clear that this chapter reveals entering the Buddha's knowledge and vision. Now the World-Honored One's answer gives few means of obtaining it, and it does not lie in many kalpas of cultivation; it is accomplished solely by accomplishing four dharmas, and after the Tathāgata's extinction one shall obtain this sutra — that is all. The four dharmas are: one, being protected and remembered by the Buddhas; two, planting the roots of all virtues; three, entering the company of the rightly settled; four, arousing the mind to save all living beings. Accomplishing these four dharmas, after the Tathāgata's extinction one will certainly obtain this sutra. And since he says shall obtain and again will certainly obtain, these are words of truth, decisiveness, and immutability. Yet what is the meaning of these four dharmas, that accomplishment should be so swift?
