The Awakening of Faith says: in distinguishing the marks of the path of aspiration, meaning the path realized by all Buddhas and the meaning of all bodhisattvas arousing the mind and aspiring toward it, it briefly says there are three kinds of arousing the mind: first, arousing the mind through accomplished faith; second, arousing the mind through understanding and practice; third, arousing the mind through realization. Because it was said earlier: if you can believe and accept these words, you shall all attain the Buddha-way; and again: you, Śāriputra, entered even this sutra through faith. Yet this sutra, the profound secret treasury of the Buddhas' knowledge and vision, is not measured by mind; it is only permitted to be entered through faith. Seen in this light, these four dharmas are the arousing of the mind through accomplished faith. The Avataṃsaka says: knowing all dharmas as the self-nature of mind, one accomplishes the body of wisdom and attains bodhi not through another's awakening — this is what is meant by the accomplishment of faith. The treatise says: one who arouses the mind through accomplished faith — what mind does he arouse? Briefly, there are three kinds. First, the straight mind, because he rightly recollects the dharma of true suchness — this is what is meant by being protected and remembered by the Buddhas. Second, the profound mind, because he delights in gathering all good practices — this is what is meant by planting the roots of all virtues. Third, the mind of great compassion, because he wishes to pull all living beings out of suffering — this is what is meant by arousing the mind to save all living beings. It also says: one who thus accomplishes faith and arouses the mind enters the company of the rightly settled, never retrogresses, and is named as dwelling in the Tathāgata's seed, corresponding to the right cause — this is what is meant by entering the company of the rightly settled. Since it is permitted to enter through faith, one then uses the power of Mañjuśrī's great wisdom, calm abiding and insight, to illumine the source of one's own mind, truly believing in mind-only with no outer realm; investigating and exhausting it thus is called wondrous practice. With this wondrous practice one accords with wondrous wisdom; wisdom and practice are wondrously perfect — this is what is meant by corresponding to the right cause. That one will certainly obtain this sutra is fitting. Thus the preceding opening of understanding and practice does not go beyond faith; when faith is ultimate the path is perfect, and one enters wondrous enlightenment. This is precisely what is meant by lighting the lamp at the eastern shrine: the fullness of wisdom is not different from the initial mind. This wondrously accords with the Avataṃsaka's beginning and end being not two. What Samantabhadra encourages is solely this faith; hence he speaks of the way to obtain the sutra, and the Tathāgata shows him only these four dharmas. It also says: when this bodhisattva's merit is complete, at the summit of form he manifests the highest and greatest body in all the world. By the wisdom corresponding to a single thought, ignorance is suddenly exhausted and it is named the wisdom of all modes; naturally there is inconceivable karma able to manifest in the ten directions to benefit living beings. Therefore after the Tathāgata's extinction, if there is one who can uphold this sutra, I shall guard him, and with the assembly of great bodhisattvas manifest my own body, making offerings and consoling his mind. If that person forgets or loses a single sentence or verse, I shall teach him and cause him to be fluent again. The treatise says: when the bodhisattva's ground is exhausted and the expedients are fulfilled, at the single thought's correspondence the mind of awakening first arises, without an initial mark, because he is far from subtle thoughts, and he gains sight of the mind-nature; hence it says: he gains sight of my body. It also says: from the bodhisattva's first aspiration up to the bodhisattva's ultimate ground, what the mind sees is named the reward-body. This is what is meant by manifesting before that person the body that all living beings delight to see and teaching him the Dharma — precisely empowerment by manifesting body, face, and speech. It also says: if a living being can contemplate no-thought, he is oriented toward the Buddha-wisdom. Hence it says: because he sees me, he at once attains samādhi and dhāraṇī, named the turning dhāraṇī, the hundred thousand myriad koṭis of turning dhāraṇīs, and the dhāraṇī of the expedient means of dharma-sound. This is the ultimate actual realization. The Sanskrit dhāraṇī is rendered here as total retention: retaining all dharmas and holding immeasurable meanings — another name for the one mind's true suchness. The treatise says: the mind's true suchness is the substance of the great total-mark Dharma-gate of the one Dharma-realm. The mind-nature is unborn and unceasing; all dharmas have differences only in dependence on deluded thoughts. If one is apart from mind-thought, there are no marks of any realm. Therefore all dharmas, from the beginning, are apart from the mark of speech, apart from the mark of names, apart from the mark of mental conditions, ultimately equal, without change, indestructible; they are only the one mind. Hence it is named true suchness. This is what is meant by the turning dhāraṇī. It also says: all speech is nominal and without reality, only following deluded thoughts and unobtainable — this is what is meant by the hundred thousand myriad koṭis of turning dhāraṇīs. It also says: as for true suchness, it too has no mark; it is the limit of speech, using words to dispel words. This substance of true suchness has nothing that can be dispelled, because all dharmas are equally true and equally such. Know that all dharmas cannot be spoken and cannot be thought; hence they are named true suchness. This is what is meant by the dhāraṇī of the expedient means of dharma-sound. As for turning: the Śūraṃgama's perfect penetration of Avalokiteśvara by the ear-faculty says: turning back the mechanism of hearing, returning to hear the self-nature. Turning is a whirlpool: where the water's swift current is deepest there is an eddy, called a swirl; meeting the swift current, its force can turn the flow back to the swirl's source. That is, within the swift current of thought-by-thought arising and ceasing, one can thought by thought accord with true suchness and not be carried along by deluded thoughts — hence like the water's swirl. The treatise says: if one knows that all dharmas, though spoken, have nothing that can speak or be spoken, and though thought, have nothing that can think or be thought, this is named accordance; being apart from thought is named entering. Now the thoughtless is right thought. Hence the final admonition is that one should single-mindedly uphold, read, recite, rightly recollect, and practice in accordance with the teaching. Right recollection is the root of all practices and the utmost of faith. Therefore whoever upholds, reads, recites, rightly recollects, understands its purport, and practices in accordance with the teaching — know that such a person practices Samantabhadra's practice. Because the One Vehicle's true mark, the Buddha's knowledge and vision, is exhaustively set forth here, and the dharmakāya's life of wisdom is not outside it, Samantabhadra vows to guard this sutra with spiritual power and, after the Tathāgata's extinction, to cause it to spread widely within Jambudvīpa, never letting it be cut off. And the Tathāgata immediately granted it, saying: whoever upholds, receives, reads, recites, rightly recollects, cultivates, and copies this Lotus Sutra — know that such a person sees Śākyamuni Buddha and hears this sutra as if from the Buddha's own mouth; with all manner of praise, before long he shall attain bodhi. The swiftness of its effect being thus, and the weight of evil retribution for those who do not believe and lightly slander it being likewise, it finally grants that one enters through faith. This is what is meant by: faith is the mother of the virtues, the source of the path, nurturing all good dharmas. Only this profound secret treasury, the supreme Dharma-gate, is permitted to be entered through faith. It is precisely said: the initial and ultimate arousal of the mind are in the end not two; of these two minds, the former is the harder. Therefore this sutra takes Mañjuśrī as the leader of the chanting and Samantabhadra as the conclusion of the encouragement. This is the utmost of the Tathāgata's teaching, one from beginning to end.

In the spring of the yiwei year of Wanli I suffered calamity for spreading the Dharma and was arrested and imprisoned. Chan Master Daguan was at Mount Kuanglu; when the news reached him he was astonished and sighed, and vowed to recite the Wondrous Dharma Lotus Sutra a hundred times, seeking the Buddhas' spiritual power to receive and protect me. Soon afterward I received imperial grace and pardon and was sent to Leiyang. That winter, passing through Baixia, Master Da waited for me on the river, and we met at the Thatched Hut of Traveling and Lodging. Talking of this in the middle of the night, he said: may I use your tongue with my mind? I laughed and assented. In the spring of the bingshen year I reached the place of exile, just when famine and calamity prevailed, so that I could not settle anywhere; and I was then occupied with the Laṅkāvatāra and moreover hurrying about among the ranks, with no leisure to finish this case. Yet within the white-ray light I never departed from the samādhi of the abode of innumerable meanings. In the summer of the wuxu year, more than ten disciples under the bodhi tree came to follow me in my wanderings, and together we kept the summer retreat in a domed hut, reciting this sutra nearly two hundred times. From time to time I raised this matter for them and instructed them. On the day of the summer's end and self-indulgence, my disciple Xingcheng asked me to explain its essential purport; so I plucked out the purport of our Buddha beyond words and showed it to them, and would thereby repay Master Da, letting him know that the Wondrous Dharma Lotus Sutra I turn is no more than this. Old Lu said: when the mind is deluded, the Lotus turns the mind; when the mind is awakened, the mind turns the Lotus. Yet the one phrase that does not touch the lips lies precisely not among paper, ink, and letters. Then those present at the hearing each rejoiced, believed, accepted, and practiced accordingly. It was cut in wood to spread the gift of Dharma, with the universal vow that all who see, hear, and rejoice may alike attain the samādhi that manifests all physical forms. Written on the last day of the wuxu year of Wanli by the Daoist Hanshan, Deqing, in the Laṅkāvatāra Chamber.
The Dream-Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Scroll Forty-Three
Supplement to the General Commentary on the Śūraṃgama Sutra

The Śūraṃgama Sutra as a whole gathers up the teaching of one entire age: delusion and awakening, cultivation and realization, cause and fruit; it directly cuts off the root of birth and death, the two kinds of ignorance that produce karma and moisten rebirth, named the continuity of becoming; it suddenly breaks the three parts of the eighth consciousness, and therefore sets up three kinds of wondrous contemplation, gathering them back into the great Śūraṃgama samādhi. This is the supreme One Vehicle, the perfect and sudden Dharma-gate, directly revealing the one true Dharma-realm. The Tathāgatagarbha nature is called the wondrous perfect true mind. It is in dependence on this great samādhi that three contemplations are arrayed, because the Tathāgatagarbha has three meanings: the empty Tathāgatagarbha, the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, and the Tathāgatagarbha that is neither empty nor non-empty. Through this nature of the treasury, deluded, it becomes the ālaya-consciousness and transforms into the two parts of seeing and marks; the nature of the treasury, as it exists in the consciousness, is named the part of self-realization. Because its intrinsic nature is undefiled it is named the pure white consciousness, which is the part of the realization of self-realization. According to the treatise's two gates of true suchness and arising-and-ceasing, this part of the realization of self-realization is precisely true suchness; its part of self-realization is the inherent awakening amid delusion; the seeing-part is the first seven turning consciousnesses; the mark-part is empty space and the four elements — outwardly the world, mountains, rivers, and the great earth, and the five dust-objects; inwardly the faculty-body, the form and feeling aggregates of the five aggregates that are grasped and received. The 'seeing' is the seventh consciousness, the mind-root, together with the sixth mind-consciousness, the first five consciousnesses, and the simultaneously discriminating mind-consciousness. Now the cultivation of the great Śūraṃgama samādhi lies precisely in directly breaking the eighth consciousness. But this consciousness-substance has long been deluded, and through the two parts of marks and seeing it binds itself into the faculty-body of the five aggregates and the five dust-objects of the outer world, becoming the coarse and subtle attachments to self and dharma, both discriminated and innate. Clinging to the faculty-body of the five aggregates is the attachment to self; craving the outer five dust-objects as what I enjoy and positing something done is the attachment to dharma. Through these two attachments one is tangled in birth and death. Therefore, now wishing to escape birth and death, one must first break the two attachments as the initial expedient. Hence Ānanda specifically requested the wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna as the essentials of Buddhahood, and the Buddha specifically granted him the samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṃgama King. This was a request made in successive terms, while the Buddha taught in terms of the one mind's perfect and interfused great samādhi. Know then that this sutra, from beginning to end, does not go beyond the three contemplations, and ultimately does not depart from the one mind. Though the sutra text does not explicitly state the destination, in its passages of breaking and revealing it is luminously clear; only those who circulate it have not investigated it. The three contemplations are: the sutra's wondrous śamatha corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness; samādhi corresponds to the contemplation of the provisional; dhyāna corresponds to the contemplation of the middle way. All are called wondrous to show the perfect and interfused three contemplations, wondrously according with the one mind: raise one and there are three, speak of three and it is one; apart from affirmation and apart from negation, utterly beyond the reach of thought and speech. Now in discussing this sutra, I mark it out throughout by substance, mark, and function, intending that one first awakens and afterward cultivates; hence the substance of contemplation is marked first, wishing one first to awaken to the principle-substance of the treasury-nature's three truths, and in dependence on it to establish the marks of contemplation — what is meant by first awakening to the Vairocana Dharma-realm. Next the marks of contemplation are shown, the meaning being that the markless true mind is now wholly deluded into consciousness and binds itself into the five aggregates, faculty-body, and world, dharmas that have marks; the essential point is to cultivate within marks. Hence in the passage on cultivation it points solely to the five aggregates and six faculties, and next to the three categories and seven elements, each and every one a gate of awakening and entry. In the section on realizing the fruit, the function of contemplation is marked, precisely revealing that the three contemplations cultivated possess the power to sever and to realize. Hence what I call 'from beginning to end not going beyond the three contemplations' is this.

Question: Why are the three contemplations divided into substance, mark, and function? Answer: Though they are named three contemplations, this is in terms of the principle of the Tathāgatagarbha's three truths, which must be realized by the three contemplations; in reality they are altogether the one mind. Hence the Buddha granted the great Śūraṃgama samādhi, meaning that the three contemplations do not depart from the one mind. According to the Awakening of Faith: there is a dharma that can arouse the root of Mahāyāna faith. The dharma spoken of is the mind of living beings; this mind altogether contains all mundane and supramundane dharmas, and so it is not named mind but named dharma. Now where there is a dharma there must be meanings, and substance, mark, and function make three meanings of the one mind — what are called the three greatnesses. This true mind's substance is vast, hence it is called the greatness of substance. Because it is originally markless, yet now manifests the phenomena of the ten dharma-realms, their principal and dependent causes and fruits, all dharmas that have marks, its mark is likewise great. Because deluding this mind makes the six ordinary destinies and awakening to this mind makes the four sagehoods, all being the wondrous function of the one mind's transformation, its function is likewise great. The intent is that one first awaken to the substance of this mind; the Buddha calls this opening and showing this substance, so as to make cultivation possible. Hence the substance of contemplation is clarified first. Having awakened to this substance and understood that the faculty-body, world, and all deluded marks are established in dependence on the one mind, one now illumines and breaks through each deluded mark with the substance one has awakened to, since they are originally the wondrous luminous true mind. Hence cultivation proceeds only within deluded marks; this is called the marks of contemplation, and it is precisely the essential point of cultivating the path. The fifty-five stages are all established in dependence on the contemplation of mind, the essential point being to reveal that these three contemplations possess the great function of severing delusion and realizing truth; hence they are the function of the three contemplations. Using the treatise to assess the sutra, the text is clear and evident and wondrously accords with the Buddha-mind; hence my judgment and arrangement are without doubt, revealing the Tathāgata's original intent in teaching the Dharma and making it easy for practitioners to enter.

Question: Within the substance of the three contemplations, the text of three and a half scrolls of the sutra is gathered; and the one section of the contemplation of emptiness alone covers three scrolls of sutra text. As for the three categories and seven elements being originally the Tathāgatagarbha, this seems to reveal the principle of emptiness. Why then does it begin with the investigation of mind and the discernment of seeing, and proceed through the two kinds of deluded views and their various examinations and disputations? Answer: This sutra gathers up the five teachings, and this one substance of the contemplation of emptiness completely contains the principle of emptiness of the five teachings, penetrating the discourse of an entire age. The text is concise and the meaning profound, exceedingly hard to comprehend; hence in my general commentary I have fully set out the outline of the passages of breaking and revealing, so that the essential points may be known. As for breaking delusion and revealing truth, the sutra text is only a scroll and a half, yet its meaning has already gathered up the teaching set forth in the preceding forty years — it is no shallow matter. Our Buddha appeared in the world and taught the Dharma for forty-nine years, delivering more than three hundred assemblies, solely to break living beings' two attachments to self and dharma. If the two attachments are broken, one realizes nirvāṇa; nirvāṇa is the quiescent one mind of the Tathāgatagarbha. Because living beings delude this Tathāgatagarbha mind, the unborn-and-unceasing joins with arising-and-ceasing to form the ālaya-consciousness. This consciousness possesses four parts: first, the part of the realization of self-realization, which is the one mind's true suchness; second, the part of self-realization, which is the inherent awakening amid delusion, corresponding to the treatise's meaning of enlightenment and non-enlightenment; third, the seeing-part, which is the first seven turning consciousnesses; fourth, the mark-part, which is the outer world. In the sutra, earth, water, fire, wind, and empty space are the outer five great elements, and the faculty-body within the world is the five-aggregate living being. Because living beings have deluded this true mind, they merely recognize the illusory, deluded body of the five aggregates as their own body and mind, falsely clinging to it as self — this is named the discriminated attachment to self. The five dust-objects of the outer world as what I enjoy is named the discriminated attachment to dharma. These two discriminated attachments are both posited by the sixth consciousness; since the seventh consciousness is the root of the sixth, turning according to the inner and outer gates, in fact the two consciousnesses posit them together. There are also the innate attachments to self and dharma; these belong solely to the seventh consciousness, which posits the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness as the inner self — the attachment to self — and posits cultivation and false attainment as the attachment to dharma. These two are subtle and are named the two innate attachments. If both kinds of two attachments are utterly broken, one may realize and enter the source of the one mind; this is named Buddha. Since Ānanda had deluded the true mind and was bound by the two obstructions, they had to be utterly broken before there could be the true path of bodhi. Hence these three contemplations are the instruments for breaking the coarse and subtle two attachments. The passages investigating mind and discerning seeing break through the coarse and subtle two kinds of attachment to self and the two kinds of deluded view; and the later breaking of conjunction breaks through the coarse and subtle two kinds of attachment to dharma. For this great Śūraṃgama samādhi perfectly severs the five abiding afflictions and equally ends the two kinds of birth and death, unlike other sutras that have a sequence. Because it gathers up the five teachings and suddenly realizes the one mind, it does not establish a sequence.

Question: The various teachings speak separately of first severing the two discriminated attachments and next severing the two innate attachments; why does this text speak of severing them all at once? Answer: The seventh consciousness is the root of the two attachments to self and dharma, turning according to the inner and outer gates. If it turns by the outer gate and serves as the root of the sixth consciousness, there are the two discriminated attachments. If it turns by the inner gate, it clings to the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness as self — this is the innate attachment to self, and this attachment is severed only at the seventh ground. Above the eighth ground there remains the innate attachment to dharma, because the seventh consciousness possesses the meaning of the two parts, defiled and pure; hence what is severed at the seventh ground is the defiled portion of manas. What formerly clung to the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness as self — now that this defiled portion is once severed, the name of storehouse consciousness is abandoned, and this eighth consciousness is turned to realize true suchness and is named the pure white consciousness. There still remains the pure portion of manas, which clings to this true suchness as what I have realized — this is the subtle attachment to dharma. Thus the later sutra says: when the bodhi-mind arises and the mind of arising-and-ceasing ceases, this still belongs to arising and ceasing. Because one clings to true suchness as something realized, with subject and object not yet forgotten and the contemplation-wisdom not yet dissolved, this is still the subtle attachment to dharma. If this attachment is severed, one then enters wondrous enlightenment and realizes the source of the one mind. This meaning wholly accords with the Awakening of Faith; the assessment is most clear. Hence it is said to be sudden severing and sudden realization.

Question: The passages of this sutra that break attachment were previously unclear; the transmitters of old merely said that it investigates mind and discerns seeing, and as for the two kinds of deluded views, they did not know why these were taught either. Now, though my general commentary clearly sets out the sections of breaking and revealing, which are precisely the meaning of breaking attachment, the sequence of before and after is still not clear. Pray explain in detail. Answer: The coarse and subtle two attachments spoken of pertain to the two paths of the true and the false, and altogether do not go beyond the eight consciousnesses and five aggregates. What the teaching of an entire age breaks is nothing but this. Because the one mind is deluded, it becomes the ālaya-consciousness; this consciousness possesses four parts, and its first three parts are the body, mind, and world of the five aggregates, while its part of the realization of self-realization is the true suchness realized. Now the coarse and subtle two attachments break only the four parts of consciousness-only, gathering them back into the one mind as the ultimate. Hence, assessing the sutra text, the breaking proceeds accordingly: first the five aggregates are broken, belonging to the discriminated attachment to self, and in the breaking of the aggregate of consciousness the innate attachment to self is carried along within it; the two kinds of deluded views break the discriminated attachment to dharma, which ordinary beings and the Two Vehicles cling to in common; hence after breaking the two delusions the inherent true mind of awakening is revealed. From this one knows that the innate attachment to self has already been broken along the way. As for the next chapter's saying: though you have first awakened to the inherent luminous mind of awakening, you have not yet understood that this source of awakening is neither born of conjunction nor of non-conjunction — this precisely breaks the innate attachment to dharma. Thus the later sutra says: when the bodhi-mind arises and the mind of arising-and-ceasing ceases, this still belongs to arising and ceasing. Once this attachment is broken, one at once returns to the treasury-nature. Hence the following text explains that each and every one is the Tathāgatagarbha, the intent being to show that what was revealed by the earlier breaking was mere emptiness; the later passages that gather the three categories and seven elements reveal the meaning of wondrous existence, the true mark, and true emptiness. This is truly the key to breaking delusion; examine it carefully and deeply, and its wonder will appear.

Question: In the passages that break attachment, though the sections are divided, the sequence along the way is not yet clear; pray explain in detail. Answer: The two discriminated attachments are what all living beings cling to — the body, mind, and world of the five aggregates — and these belong to the two parts of seeing and marks of the eighth consciousness. The innate attachment to self is the part of self-realization of the eighth consciousness, which the seventh consciousness has inwardly clung to as self. This self is the essence of seeing in the sutra, namely the substance of self-realization, the inherent Buddha-nature of awakening amid delusion. Hence once the two delusions in the sutra are broken, this inherent true mind of awakening is revealed; this belongs to the conditional Buddha-nature, revealed through severing, and is not yet the true suchness free of obstruction. For the pure portion of manas still clings to this awakening as what I have realized — this is precisely the subtle attachment to dharma, what is meant by the attachment to dharma unforgotten and self-view still remaining. The bodhisattva of the eighth ground in the Avataṃsaka is deluded within the principle of true suchness and must await the three bridges and seven exhortations before he can relinquish it, because the ripened consciousness is not yet empty; this shows it is the hardest to sever. Advancing from the eighth ground into Equal Enlightenment corresponds to this sutra's passage after the two delusions where the Buddha says: though you have first awakened to the inherent luminous mind of awakening, you have not yet understood that this source of awakening is neither born of conjunction nor non-conjunction. The intent is to break the awakening of conjunction, meaning that when initial awakening accords with inherent awakening it is named ultimate awakening, yet this still belongs to conjunction and duality; hence once this conjunction is broken, the Tathāgatagarbha nature is revealed and one suddenly realizes the source of the one mind. Know therefore that above the eighth ground one breaks the innate attachment to dharma; this is where the treatise's statement that the Buddha possesses the pure portion of manas belongs. As for the passages breaking the two discriminated attachments, from the initial request for samādhi until after the breaking of the essence of seeing, they break throughout the body and mind of the five aggregates, and the innate attachment to self is also among what is broken; the passage on the two delusions breaks solely the discriminated attachment to dharma. Its purport is most clear.

Question: In the initial breaking of the five aggregates, the Tathāgata first approaches it through the investigation of mind, yet the section is said to break the aggregates of form and feeling; the meaning is still unclear. Pray show it directly. Answer: The two parts of marks and seeing of the eighth consciousness: marks are the four elements, seeing is the turning consciousness. With the initial seeing-part it takes a small portion of the four elements as my faculty-body — what the treatise points to as the place of grasping and receiving — and thus becomes the living being of the five aggregates. Hence the sutra says: once deluded into mind, one is decisively deluded into being within the form-body. This is that. Because the aggregates of form and feeling are precisely where grasping and receiving depend, though it is named the investigation of mind, the intent is to show that this faculty-body is fundamentally empty and not a place to depend on; one who would cultivate the great samādhi must first inwardly free himself from body and mind. Hence the aggregates of form and feeling are broken first; once the form-body is broken there is nothing grasped or received, and the deluded mind has no support. Therefore the next step breaks the sixth consciousness as the aggregate of imagination.

Question: After the investigation of mind, Ānanda again requests the path of śamatha, and the Tathāgata emits light and questions his mind again; the section is said to break the aggregate of imagination of the sixth consciousness. Why? Answer: The initial investigation of mind is to break the aggregates of form and feeling, precisely breaking the Small Vehicle's view of the body, the intent being to show that one who would cultivate the great samādhi must inwardly free himself from the faculty-body. Because ordinary beings merely recognize deluded thought as mind, and non-Buddhists rely on this, falsely positing the Small Vehicle's mere severing of the sixth consciousness and the gods of the two upper realms' mere extinguishing of the sixth consciousness, the Buddha says at the very outset: all living beings, by clinging to this deluded thought of birth and death, mistake it for the real; though they speak of cultivation, they do not accomplish the sage-fruit. Hence one who cultivates the great samādhi must first break it. Because this deluded thought has always clung to this faculty-body as its place of dependence, and one raises this clinging mind as being within this body, it is questioned by the Buddha; hence there are the seven successive clingings, all now broken, and it has been shown that the four elements are fundamentally empty — the aggregates of form and feeling are already empty. Only this deluded thought is the root of birth and death, so it is broken next. The intent is to show that this imagination cannot be broken without the contemplation of emptiness; hence Ānanda again requests the instruction on the path of śamatha. Before breaking it, the Buddha emits light, meaning to take this light as the substance of samādhi: one who understands this light has deluded thought suddenly broken, without need of words. Because living beings are blind to this light and merely use deluded thought in all manner of inversion, the two kinds of inversion are marked first as the root of what is to be broken; it is said that when inversion does not arise, that is the Tathāgata's true samādhi. Hence what is broken below is the two inversions. He still questions his mind because it is the inverted mind; and because the inverted mind gives rise to inverted views, he raises his fist and tests both mind and eye as to where they are. Ānanda clings only to the discriminating deluded thought as mind, so the Buddha rebukes it as not the mind, concluding: it is all because you cling to this deluded thought of birth and death, and so on. This precisely breaks the sixth consciousness as the aggregate of imagination. The following text then breaks the inverted views, so Ānanda again requests the revealing of the wondrous mind and the opening of his eye of the path, the intent being to break deluded views.

Question: In the passage breaking seeing, I do not know where it comes to rest; pray explain in detail. Answer: Seeing is the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness, which is the first seven turning consciousnesses; the seventh consciousness is the mind-root of the sixth, and so the seventh turns according to the inner and outer gates. Turning outward in the sixth consciousness it is the discriminated view; turning inward it clings to the eighth consciousness as self, which is the inferential view — there is only the difference of coarse and subtle. First the ordinary being's eternalist view, the Two Vehicles' nihilist view, and the non-Buddhist's annihilationist view are broken, all of them breaking the discriminated view, belonging to the first inversion and still tied to the sixth consciousness. Hence the later text belongs to the seventh consciousness, the aggregate of formations, breaking the inferential view, which belongs to the second inversion. Now the discriminated view is the discriminated attachment to self, and the inferential view is the innate attachment to self, which is fully broken only when the essence of consciousness is broken. Those two kinds of deluded view break the discriminated attachment to dharma; and the chapter on breaking conjunction after the two delusions breaks the innate attachment to dharma. Because in realizing true suchness, if subject and object are not yet dissolved and there is something realized, this is the subtle attachment to dharma; the section is titled 'sweeping away traces and entering the profound,' the intent being to dissolve the contemplating mind and cut off all duality. Once these two attachments are broken, one at once returns to the one mind; hence the following passages on the three categories and seven elements are each and every one originally the Tathāgatagarbha.

Question: In the passage breaking seeing, the section joins the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, which seems tangled and hard for students to distinguish; pray point it out. Answer: The three parts of the eighth consciousness are present in every consciousness, and the seeing-part is the first seven turning consciousnesses. Hence the treatise says: able to manifest, able to see, able to grasp objects — so both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses possess seeing. The views of ordinary beings, the Two Vehicles, and non-Buddhists that lie in the sixth consciousness are precisely what can grasp objects; this is called the discriminated view, which the treatise calls the objective condition at a distance. The seventh consciousness, discussed in terms of the eight returnings, precisely points to what can see — the inferential view, which is exactly spoken of in relation to the mark-part. What breaks the measure of seeing is discussed in terms of what can manifest; because it is what manifests the mark-part and gives rise to seeing, it still belongs to the seventh consciousness. Once this measure is broken, only then are the two parts dissolved and one returns to the essence of seeing. The Buddha's intent is most profound and subtle, and cannot be understood without subtle, secret contemplation; because this lies at the gate of breaking delusion, one should search and unfold it in detail — it is by no means a tangled teaching.

Question: In the passage breaking seeing, first the eight returnings are discussed and the section is called 'selecting conditions,' and afterward the essence of seeing is revealed and the section is also called 'selecting conditions.' The sutra's meaning differs, yet the section is the same — why? Answer: Though the section 'selecting conditions' is the same, the meaning is also distinct. The former selecting of conditions is because the seeing-part is mixed among conditioning dust, with subject and object never distinguished; hence the seven conditions are selected as the conditioning dust-objects, and in distinguishing conditions subject and object are specifically separated, each having its own return. Yet the nature of seeing is not absent: it means that whatever can be returned is not seeing, and what cannot be returned is the nature of seeing. This only provisionally separates subject and object and does not yet exactly point to the nature of seeing as the essence of seeing. The second, revealing the essence of seeing and selecting conditions, selects only the mark-part, the conditioning shadows manifested by the eighth consciousness, without speaking of the seeing-part. The meaning is that all images of things are manifested within the substance of the eighth consciousness, like a scene in a mirror, scene and mirror undivided; hence the condition of the direct mark-part is selected away, and the seeing-part dissolves of itself while the consciousness-substance remains — hence it is the essence of seeing, the perfect luminosity of the essence of consciousness. This is to dissolve throughout the two parts of marks and seeing and point solely to the consciousness-substance as the essence of seeing. This meaning is profound and hidden, not to be grasped by a coarse mind; it must be examined subtly.

Question: The measure of seeing seems to belong to the eighth consciousness's direct perception; hence once this is broken it is said that body and mind are perfect and luminous, the site of awakening unmoving, and that within a single hair-tip one can contain and receive the lands of the ten directions — this has already reached the ultimate. Why then is there later text breaking self and so forth in terms of the eighth consciousness? Answer: Though the measure of seeing resembles the eighth consciousness's direct perception, the consciousness that can manifest the two parts of seeing and marks is said by the treatise to be the direct objective condition; if seeing and marks are not yet dissolved and duality is not yet forgotten, it must belong to the seventh consciousness. The passage revealing the true, where body and mind are perfect and luminous, is precisely in terms of breaking defiled non-knowledge, so that one does not grasp body and mind; hence it says perfect and luminous. A single hair-tip containing and receiving the lands of the ten directions precisely shows freedom from measure, hence without obstruction; this is a partial seeing of the true principle, and in fact is not yet the ultimate. The commentary is most clear; examine it carefully.

Question: The Buddha points to the essence of seeing as a second moon, and says that though it is not the wondrous pure luminous mind it is like a second moon. Why is it that just when the essence of seeing is revealed, before the eighth consciousness is broken, the sutra says that if one can turn things one is the same as the Tathāgata, and within a single hair-tip can contain and receive the lands of the ten directions? If the revealed principle is already thorough, why is it possible while the eighth consciousness is not yet broken? Answer: This is not knowable by shallow wisdom. Take the bodhisattva of the first ground: he has just broken the two discriminated attachments while the storehouse consciousness remains entirely, yet he can see a hundred Buddha-worlds; thereafter, ground by ground advancing, what he sees gradually becomes vast — is this not a single hair-tip containing and receiving the lands of the ten directions? Moreover, this consciousness-substance is itself true suchness, and is only obstructed by the two parts of seeing and marks. Now that the two parts are dissolved, the essence of consciousness is perfect and luminous, and the lands of the ten directions are luminously pure: how could a hair-tip containing the ten directions be in doubt?

Question: The turning of 'if one can turn things' — is it the same as the turning of 'turning consciousness into wisdom,' or different? Answer: Though the word turning is the same, what is turned is greatly different. In turning consciousness into wisdom, each of the eight consciousnesses has its own turning, with sequence and precedence, spoken of solely in terms of consciousness. In this sutra's turning of things, no turning of consciousness is spoken of; it is only in terms of turning things. When things are turned, the seeing-part dissolves as well; and once the seeing-part dissolves, the first seven consciousnesses turn all at once, originally without sequence or precedence. Because seeing is the mark of activity of the eighth consciousness's discernment, and the first seven turning consciousnesses are established in dependence on this seeing, when seeing dissolves the seven consciousnesses turn together. The reason is this: the mark-only school takes consciousness as the root, while this sutra gathers marks back to nature and specifically manifests the mind-only realm, taking the one mind's true source as the root. Because the one mind's true suchness is deluded into the ālaya-consciousness, there are the two parts of seeing and marks; and since the mark-part is established, the seeing-part grasps the mark-part and becomes a living being — what is called the self-mind grasping the self-mind, the non-illusory becoming illusory dharmas. Now that the seeing-part is dissolved, one is free of grasping; hence every dharma is fundamentally true and each is originally the Tathāgatagarbha, turning of itself without needing to be turned. This is what is meant by: no need to seek the true; one need only put an end to views. Once the seeing-part dissolves, the mark-part turns of itself into the one mind's true suchness; hence one is the same as the Tathāgata. This is what is meant by: not grasping, there is nothing that is not illusory; the non-illusory does not even arise — how could illusory dharmas stand? This meaning is profound and hidden, and only subtle, secret contemplation can know it.

Question: I already know the meaning of breaking seeing. As for the passages breaking the eighth consciousness, it first says breaking self and has one infer from things, then has Mañjuśrī select by right and wrong; in breaking self-realization it breaks by spontaneity and causality; and in breaking the essence of consciousness it again selects by brightness, darkness, form, and emptiness — and each section is titled 'to reveal the one true.' Is this not repetition? Answer: It is not repetition. Because the Tathāgata teaches specifically to break living beings' false clinging, and the various inversions spoken of earlier show that living beings' false positing is not of one kind. His teaching is not like Chan, where one awakening is the end; in the teachings one must search and unfold in detail, for within delusion there are naturally all kinds of false positings, and each must be spoken of and broken. As for breaking self: because the Two Vehicles cling to this eighth consciousness as the nirvāṇa-self, and before awakening posit the aggregates as identical with or separate from self, non-Buddhists posit it as the spirit-self, and living beings generally posit it as the self of birth and death — so now, wishing to break this consciousness, he first breaks their view of self. This is precisely the innate attachment to self. As for having one infer right and wrong from things: because this consciousness-substance wholly transforms into the deluded imaginings of faculty-body and world, fundamentally without a second dharma, he has one infer right and wrong from things, the essential point being to reveal that they are originally one true; hence he has Mañjuśrī unfold it to cut off views of right and wrong and awaken to the principle of the one true. As for breaking self-realization by spontaneity and causality: because non-Buddhists, not knowing this consciousness, falsely posit that dharmas arise spontaneously — called self-arising without cause — or that dharmas arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions — called co-arising and other-arising — all not knowing that the self-substance of the eighth consciousness is originally the wondrous awakened luminous mind. Hence he breaks it by spontaneity and causality; once this positing is broken, the subtle awakening reveals itself. As for breaking the essence of seeing, this is precisely the essence of consciousness, originally luminous, able to produce all conditions, what is left behind by conditions, as set out in the two inversions above; hence he pursues and breaks all delusions, and only here breaks it. Again, he takes brightness, darkness, form, and emptiness because this precisely reveals that the essence of consciousness can produce all conditions and is what conditions leave behind; hence he selects conditions to break it, the essential point being to be free of conditions to reveal the true mind. This is truly the ultimate in breaking consciousness. And every section is titled 'revealing the true' because in breaking those false positings their truth is revealed — but this is partial revelation, not the whole. The Buddha said the ādāna-consciousness is most profound and subtle; hence it is not easily grasped by a coarse mind. Examine it deeply.

Question: In the passage breaking the essence of seeing, it again breaks in terms of the former dust of brightness, darkness, form, and emptiness, and says 'it is said that I can see'; and in the section revealing initial awakening it again selects conditions. How does this differ from the earlier breaking of the seeing-part and selecting conditions? Answer: This text seems the same, but its meaning is utterly different, and it is deeply hard to understand; pray set it out in detail. The former breaking of the seeing-part with the selecting of conditions is because the seeing-part grasps the grasped object-realm and has never distinguished them; hence, about to break the seeing-part, one must first select away deluded conditions. Once deluded conditions are gone, seeing has nothing to grasp, and this seeing dissolves without being dissolved — since marks are posited as existent and posited as nonexistent together. Once the two parts are dissolved, the essence of seeing stands alone; hence it is precisely broken with the words: when seeing sees, seeing is not seeing; seeing still transcends seeing and cannot reach it. And the section is called 'pointing out initial awakening' because this essence of seeing is fundamental ignorance: it means that when true seeing sees this essence of seeing, true seeing is not the essence of seeing; that is, when true wisdom illumines this ignorance, ignorance is not true wisdom. Moreover, this ignorance is transformed by true wisdom and is very close to the true, yet wisdom still transcends it; hence it says seeing still transcends seeing. How could the grasping deluded view reach it? Hence it says seeing cannot reach it. Here wisdom arises and delusion perishes; hence the section is called 'pointing out initial awakening.' As for breaking the essence of seeing and still selecting conditions, this is selecting the essence of seeing as free from conditions. It was said earlier that the essence of consciousness, originally luminous, can produce all conditions; hence only when free of conditions is the essence of seeing revealed. These conditions are the direct mark-part of the eighth consciousness, the direct objective condition; whereas the conditions selected by the earlier seeing-part are the objective condition at a distance — the former carried transformation, this one carries along. Understand this mark-only school, and the purport here becomes clear.

Question: Since the essence of seeing is broken and the wisdom of initial awakening revealed, with the five aggregates and eight consciousnesses all broken and all delusions gone, why does Ānanda still fail to open his mind regarding the positing of causality, spontaneity, and conjunction, and again increase his confusion over the seeing of seeing? Because of this he asks again below; but the World-Honored One directly teaches the two kinds of deluded view, not answering according to the question, and the section is titled 'to break the attachment to dharma.' This meaning is profound and hidden and truly hard to grasp; pray explain in detail. Answer: This secret intent has never been understood. Because the teachings say the five aggregates are both nominal and actual dharmas, all the foregoing breaking of the body and mind of the five aggregates only speaks of breaking the clinging sentiment that clings to the aggregates; what it breaks is the nominal, while the actual dharmas of the five aggregates still remain. Hence he still harbors the doubt of causality, spontaneity, and conjunction, and his mind is not yet open. As for the confusion increased over the seeing of seeing: because the essence of seeing is the self-substance of the eighth consciousness, fundamental ignorance, it is said: the subtle consciousness of ādāna, with habit becoming a torrent — true or not true, I fear confusion, and so I have never expounded it. This the World-Honored One never lightly spoke of, and hence the Two Vehicles have always been deluded about it. Now the words 'seeing of seeing is not seeing' mean that true seeing sees this essence of seeing; it is true wisdom illumining this ignorance. How could the Two Vehicles know this? Moreover, as when brightness comes darkness goes and wisdom arises delusion perishes, the true and the false cannot both stand; the sutra says this ignorance has no actual substance — how could there be a truly real ignorance standing against that wisdom? Ānanda thought there really was an essence of seeing to be seen with true seeing; now that he cannot find the essence of seeing, he is confused. Moreover this ultimate is by no means the realm of the Two Vehicles; how could he not wallow in doubt? Below, the World-Honored One's answer does not follow his doubt but directly teaches the two kinds of deluded view, because he knows Ānanda has not understood fundamental ignorance and so the actual dharmas of the five aggregates are not dissolved. Since the five aggregates remain, the mountains, rivers, and great earth of the world obstruct the eye; this is precisely the attachment to dharma unforgotten and self-view still remaining. If it were solely a matter of ignorance, the Buddha's single phrase, that this ignorance has no actual substance, would suffice; but the intent here is to break the attachment to dharma regarding body, mind, and world. Hence he sets up the hair-wheel on the lamp to illustrate that the five aggregates are false, produced by what is seen with a film in the eye. One need not argue whether the hair-wheel exists or not; one need only know it is a film in the eye, and then there is no fault of seeing. The meaning is: merely observe that the body and mind of the five aggregates are false, arising from the deluded seeing of ignorance; if one understands that ignorance is fundamentally empty, body and mind dissolve of themselves. Hence in the simile it merely says that one who knows it is a film has no fault of seeing. With this single phrase the doubt about the seeing of seeing is precisely broken. If one understands that body and mind are fundamentally empty, one may by analogy regard the world as likewise like body and mind, equally the projection of deluded karma; what doubt then about causality, spontaneity, and the seeing of seeing? This is why there is the teaching of advancing and retreating to illumine together. Hence once the two delusions are broken the inherent true mind of awakening appears at once; thus the sutra concludes: if one can keep far from all conditions of conjunction and non-conjunction, then one again extinguishes the causes of birth and death, and the pure original mind, the inherent awakening, abides forever. The section is titled 'the inherent awakening free of conditions, true suchness emerging from its entanglement' — how could this be random? The Buddha's intent is most clear; it is only that the viewer's wisdom is dim and it is not easily understood.

Question: In the later chapter of the sutra, all the expositors say it breaks conjunction again, whereas this section is titled 'sweeping away traces and entering the profound'; moreover the sutra still cites the essence of seeing. These are far apart. Pray show the essential point. Answer: The commentary is most clear. This is precisely that when initial awakening has merit the inherent awakening becomes manifest; the treatise says that when initial awakening accords with the inherent awakening it is named ultimate awakening. Now, about to reveal the one mind's true source, cutting off all duality, one must directly dissolve both contemplation and wisdom, forgetting both subject and object; hence only here is the awakening of conjunction broken. This is precisely the subtle innate attachment to dharma, named the ignorance of the mark of arising. The treatise says: this ignorance only a Buddha can understand; it is not the realm of others. Hence the Buddha spoke it without being asked. But observe that the sutra says: though you have first awakened to the inherent wondrous luminosity — this grants that he had awakened before. Then it says: you have not yet understood that this source of awakening is neither conjunction nor otherwise — the meaning is utterly clear. Below it says: you still doubt the bodhi-mind by means of worldly deluded imaginings. This precisely breaks the habit of names and phrases; hence it says he doubts bodhi by worldly deluded imagining — what is meant by using the mind of arising and ceasing to discuss perfect enlightenment, so that the nature of perfect enlightenment likewise seems to flow along. Hence this knowledge and vision must be dissolved before one enters the one mind's true source. Because the true mind and true wisdom are hard to put into words, he specifically borrows the essence of seeing to break it by analogy. And since conjunction has been broken while Ānanda again forms the view of non-conjunction, he doubts again: as I consider it, is this wondrous source of awakening neither conjoined with all conditioning dust and mental thought? Observe this: one must directly forget both mind and realm and cut off the path of words and thought before entering the wonder of the one mind.

Question: In the earlier gathering of the five aggregates, the aggregate of form is raised first as arising through deluded view, and so it is said that because the eye is fatigued one deludedly sees flowers in the sky. Now in teaching the six entrances it again takes up the earlier combination of eye and fatigue as the eye-entrance. What is the intent? Answer: This is the most extremely subtle and cannot be compared with the earlier simile. For here it speaks of the very origin of the six faculties. Because the seeing-part grasps marks and absorbs habit inward, it conjoins and binds into the five pure form-faculties, which are what the defiling dust depends on; originally there was no entrance, and only now does it first exist. The eye together with fatigue — the eye is the present eye-faculty, which is the mark-part, and fatigue is the seeing-part. Because these two parts are fundamentally nonexistent, alike the fatigue-sign of bodhi staring, the intent is to show that the consciousness-substance is deluded in dependence on awakening; hence it says the two parts are the fatigue produced by bodhi. They are manifested in dependence on consciousness and are the marks of activity of consciousness, not apart from self-realization and originally without a second substance; hence it says they are alike. Thus he takes their forming the self-substance of the six faculties as the simile, meaning that originally there are no six faculties, and only because seeing and marks first conjoin do the pure form-faculties come to be; hence he raises both together, to clarify the very beginning of the six faculties' first binding. This is why it is hard to grasp.

Question: What is the meaning of 'entrance'? Answer: The mark-only school says it is the mark-part having substance and reality, form being the place where the seeing-part relies in its thinking; regardless of near or far it is the objective condition, because all have duality and all have something depended on. Now it is said that both are without substance, being only one true suchness; hence they are originally the Tathāgatagarbha.

Question: The Awakening of Faith's three subtleties are karma, turning, and manifestation, in that order; but in this sutra the three subtleties take seeing as the mark of turning and place it third, so that manifestation comes before turning. Does this not lose the treatise's meaning? Answer: It does not lose the treatise's meaning; each has its own emphasis. The treatise's meaning speaks solely of the arising of mental dharmas: within the true realm, at first because of a single deluded movement, the perfect luminous true mind is turned into ignorance; from this ignorance the marks of discrimination and continuity appear; and if one can be free of thought one realizes the one mind. This sutra emphasizes the living being's origin of arising: because of the initial single deluded movement, the markless true mind is turned at once into deluded marks that have marks, so that empty space and the four elements take shape from this — this is having what is possessed and having marks. Because there are possessed marks, the originally possessed light of wisdom is turned into deluded seeing, a deluded knowing that grasps marks. Thereupon seeing and marks share the same one luminous awakened substance, but now mixed and undivided they become a sentient being — what is called the conjunction of form and mind becoming the living being of the five aggregates. Its emphasis is on deluded seeing and grasping as the root of the sickness of birth and death — what is called the taker of rebirths. Hence it says: the self-mind grasps the self-mind; the non-illusory becomes illusory dharmas; not grasping, there is nothing that is not illusory. Hence the patriarch said: no need to seek the true; one need only put an end to views. The treatise turns mind alone, so true cultivation lies precisely in freedom from thought; this sutra turns objects, so it says that if one can turn things one is the same as the Tathāgata, and true cultivation lies precisely in not grasping, which cuts off the root of birth and death. Hence in breaking delusion it goes straight to selecting conditions. The sutra emphasizes the grasped, so it puts marks first; the treatise emphasizes the grasper, so it puts seeing first. Thus the gateways differ and cultivation and severing also differ. Examine this deeply.
The Dream-Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Scroll Forty-Four

blocks.text: Prefatory Words on Resolving Doubts about the Great Learning, Its Outline and Items

inline.s: At nineteen I abandoned brush and inkstone; at thirty I entered the mountains and cut off letters; at fifty I was censured and, by imperial grace, exiled beyond the passes; and it is now fourteen years since. Coming and going with my bowl in Wuyang, the young men wrongly esteemed me as one who knows how to speak, and came time and again to ask about the Way; yet I had nothing at all to answer, and for empty comings and substantial goings I am ashamed indeed. Sometimes someone would look on me as a Chan man, and I was like a mute eating huangbo — nothing but bitterness. One autumn day in the jiyou year I happened to come begging, and the young men prepared an incense-offering vegetarian feast at the Dharma society. I could only hold my belly with laughter that these young men truly understood me. When the meal was done they asked for instruction, and I could only breathe out the breath of gruel and rice; so I took my shame and departed. Returning by boat to Caoxi, I reflected that these young men had fed me for no short time, and that I had never yet repaid them. When one of them asked about the chapter in which Yan Hui asks about benevolence, I could only mumble. Even when I had words, they could not be complete, and complete they could not be exhaustive; and to seek to please the minds of the many is no easy thing to speak of. Because the young men's food was hard to digest, my belly still felt full. Sleeping enough in the boat, I heard my attendant reading the Great Learning, and its clamor raised doubts in me. So I took the one chapter of the classic and, following the outline and items, set up questions and answers to settle it for myself, and further cited the chapter of Yan Hui's asking about benevolence to join and compare it. It was like wielding a butcher's knife: in two half-meals I finished it. Read aloud, it did not form sentences — it is not literature. Thinking deeply, I recalled that from childhood I had read the books of Confucius seeking the Dharma of mind directly pointed out, and that he bestowed on Yan Hui alone the true transmitted secret; for the rest he drew the bow but did not let the arrow fly. I had never known that the sage's mind-seal was fully laid bare within two hundred and fifty words. How subtle, how subtle! Was I blind? Alas, I am now sixty-four years old, and only now do I know — one may call it late. I feared that when I died it would end in obscurity; hence I hastened to tell the young men. Some of them are past half my age, some not yet half; fortunate are those who hear this — one may call it early, like a good horse seeing the shadow of the whip and going a thousand li in a breath, or like the goose-king choosing the milk. Would they not take this as the breath of gruel and rice? This was stirred up solely by the feeling of one meal. May the young men take this and feed the hungry of the world; I dare not speak of broad charity. Written two days before the Mid-Autumn of the jiyou year by the outsider Deqing, in a boat on the Xu Yang Gorge.
The Way of the Great Learning Lies in Manifesting the Luminous Virtue, in Loving the People, in Resting in the Highest Good

'The Great Learning' means the learning of the immeasurable great person. The word 'way' is like 'method.' Because what people of the world see is small, they are all petty persons and cannot be called great persons, since what they learn is all petty method. Even the various schools and the hundred thinkers, with their strange stratagems and unusual arts, are no more than the view of one bend; even if their learning succeeds, it only makes a petty person. If one is willing instead to seek within himself his own original mind-nature, then once he awakens he is at once a great person; because what he learns is great, it is called the Great Learning. The method of the Great Learning is not much at all; it does not require much knowledge or much seeing. Only three things and it is done. First, one must awaken to the substance of one's own mind; hence it says 'in manifesting the luminous virtue.' Second, one must cause everyone in the world to awaken just as I have, so that all alike are no longer of the old knowledge and vision but make a brand-new career, with no self and no other, sharing great peace; hence it says 'in loving the people.' Third, whether for oneself or for the people, one must not hastily stop halfway; everyone must reach the thoroughgoing place before letting go; hence it says 'in resting in the highest good.' If one can truly learn these three things, one is a great person. The two characters 'luminous' must be understood distinctly. The second 'luminous' is the luminous of brightness and light, pointing to the substance of one's own mind. The first 'luminous' has two meanings. If one speaks of one's own work in respect of the luminous virtue, it is the luminous of awakening to clarity: the luminous virtue is the nature I originally possess, but I have always been deluded and unaware of it, exactly like a confused man who says his own head is lost and seeks it everywhere in vain; one day he suddenly comes to himself and at once knows the original head was always there and was never lost. Everyone's self-nature is originally luminous, vast, and free, lacking not a hair; but being deluded, they all seek understanding outside in the houses of others, learning their every word, thinking that what is learned is useful. If one day one awakens to one's own nature as luminous and bright, lacking nothing at all, this is to have awakened to and made clear the luminous virtue one originally possesses; hence it says 'manifesting the luminous virtue.' To awaken to the luminous virtue is at once to be a sage. This is spoken in respect of one's own portion of the work. If one speaks in respect of the portion of loving the people, the first 'luminous' is the luminous of making bright, the meaning of proclaiming and instructing, and again the meaning of displaying and revealing, like raising the sun and moon in mid-heaven; it is the luminous of great brightness. Both meanings must be thoroughly understood. Question: what is the highest good? Answer: from ancient times everyone's knowledge and vision only knew how to walk the two roads of good and evil, and only taught people to change from evil and turn to good — this is the old knowledge and vision, and what is so extraordinary about it? They did not know that the two ends of good and evil are external dharmas of duality, having nothing whatever to do with the substance of my own nature. Hence one who does evil in the world can be changed to good, and thus a good person can be changed into an evil one — enough to show that good is not reliable. Because good does not reach the utmost, even good is not good; hence the student cannot stand firm, because it is not the place of arrival and not a place where one may rest. Seen in this light, all of it is the habit of old knowledge and vision. Now when we speak of the highest good, it is awakening to and clarifying the true substance of the self-nature, which is originally neither good nor evil. It is only a stretch of luminosity, without inside or outside, without past or present, without self or other, without right or wrong — what is called standing alone and unchanging. Not one point can be attached to it; it is swept clean of the least mote. If one uses good to break evil and, evil gone, good remains, this is still separated by a layer, for this one character 'good' is originally guest-dust, not the original host; hence it is not the ultimate place where one may rest. One need only forget both good and evil and cut off the traces of self and thing, without reliance, without light or dark, without coming or going, unmoving and unshaken; only then is it the hour of arrival. Reaching this, in oneself one sees no virtue to be made luminous, and in the people one sees no people to be renewed; merged in one whole, this is the realm of the great person. With no good to name it, it is named the highest good. To know this is first to be said to know where to rest.
The Section: Knowing Where to Rest, and Then There Is Stability; with Stability, One Can Be Still

The character 'stability' points to the substance of the self-nature, quiescent and unmoving, limpid and ever stable, not something that becomes stable after practice. But students do not penetrate the substance, which is originally ever stable, and instead go off to practice and force themselves to become stable. They only take the knowledge and vision they have acquired in a lifetime and seek stability on the two ends of good and evil, on the mind of arising and ceasing — like a monkey put into a bag, like pressing a gourd under water. Seeking stability in this way, one will not be stable to the end of one's years. Why? The fault lies in using the mind of arising and ceasing, in harboring views of good and evil, in not penetrating the substance, and in wrestling solely with deluded thoughts — what is called taking a thief for one's son, being greatly ignorant of where to rest. If one can penetrate the substance, one is at once quiescent; this is the stability of the self-nature, not a stability that can be forced. Take the Sixth Patriarch's instruction to students on how to use the mind: not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — what is the original face of the venerable one? The student at that moment cuts clean in two, and at once sees the self-nature, and the mad mind suddenly rests, never again seeking elsewhere; only then does he awaken to the fact that his own self was never moved at all. This is the very picture of knowing where to rest and then having stability. He also said: you need only not think of either good or evil, and you will naturally see the substance of mind. This is the very picture of knowing where to rest. Hence the student values knowing where to rest; knowing where to rest, he is naturally stable. The character 'still' differs from the character 'stable.' Stability is the stable substance of the self-nature; this stillness is spoken in contrast to outward disturbance and unrest, and is far indeed from the substance of stability. Why? Because the student's deluded thoughts have always been flying in confusion, and his mind cannot rest for a moment; he only strains to suppress and press down on his knowledge and vision, using the mind to enforce stillness, not knowing that the more urgently he seeks stillness the more fiercely his disordered thoughts blaze, so that he certainly cannot be still. Why? Because he uses the mind to seek the mind: the more he seeks the farther away it is, and how could he obtain a single thought of rest? Seeking to enter from outside is like a man who calls at the gate and finds it unopened, and instead falls to quarreling with the gatekeeper; the quarrel goes on to the very end, and if the true master does not appear, the brawling can never rest. But if the master opens the double gate from within, the gatekeeper flees without a trace, and the one seeking entry truly sees the master, so that the mind of seeking to see also ceases and is no more. This is what is meant by the place where the mad mind rests being stillness. If one does not truly see the substance, in the end one can never be still. Hence it says: with stability, one can be still. The character 'peace' is the meaning of steady and level, and also like the peace of accepting one's lot: being self-sufficient and seeking nothing more. Because one has always sought stillness without attaining it, with mixed thoughts in confusion and seeking that never rests, this mind has not one thought of peace. Now that the substance is awakened, the seeking mind rests, and the self-nature is complete, lacking nothing and with nothing left over, steady and level, happy and free. This peace and leisure and happiness are obtained at the place where the mad mind rests. Hence it says: with stillness, one can be at peace. The character 'consideration' is not the consideration of deluded thought or pondering, nor the consideration of anxiety; it is the consideration that does not consider. Hence it is said: the Yi is without thought, without consideration, quiescent and unmoving, yet responsive and thereby penetrating the affairs of the world. And again: a hundred considerations return to one. And again: without considering, it pervades. This is precisely this character 'consideration.' It means that before awakening one sought solely on deluded thought and pondering, so that even for a single matter one had a thousand thoughts and ten thousand considerations, and in the end it was useless and could not be considered. The more one thought and considered, the more the mind became unpeaceful. Now that one has awakened and made clear this mind, which is peaceful and free, then as thought arises and the mind stirs, all is perfect and penetrating, and the affairs of the world are clear before one's eyes. This realm is not something that clever knowledge and vision can calculate; it is the radiance of the substance of one's own mind, naturally complete. Hence it says: with peace, one can consider. The character 'attainment' is not the attainment of gain and loss; it is the meaning of without leakage. The sage responds universally and aptly, illumining all dispositions; not a hair is mistaken, the very bottom is seen through, and each thing hits the mark; hence it is called attainment — it is not that there is something attained. When one had not yet made the luminous virtue clear, one used solely deluded thought and pondering, calculating and measuring, and even when right one did not attain it, because it was not real. Now with the radiance of the self-nature one contemplates all alike and illumines all together, and the manifold dispositions and differing states all return to one principle; hence one can accomplish all in detail without omission. This is not to have attained something, for it is the consideration that does not consider and the attainment that does not attain. Hence it says: with consideration, one can attain. It means it is not an occasional hitting of the mark; it is precisely by consideration that one hits it.
The Section: The Ancients Who Wished to Make the Luminous Virtue Clear throughout the World

This explains the preceding sequence of root and branch, before and after, so as to verify the actual effect of manifesting the luminous virtue and loving the people. Spoken in terms of the work of accomplishing oneself, manifesting the luminous virtue is the root and renewing the people is the branch — this speaks from the root up to the branch. Now, spoken in terms of accomplishing things, it therefore speaks from the branch back down to the root. Previously, from the knowing where to rest of the one mind one worked up to considering and being able to attain; reaching this, all the affairs of the world return to my square inch. Now one wishes to take the luminous virtue one has awakened to and reveal it to the people of the world, wishing to make everyone awaken together. The character 'wish' is precisely the power of vow: since I have now awakened to this nature of luminous virtue, and this nature is what all people in the world equally possess and share, how could I bear to know it myself and abandon others? Therefore I vow to reveal it to the people of the world and cause them to awaken and realize together. But I fear that one who bears this vow will be thought impractical and will find it hard to obtain quick results; and the world is so vast that it cannot be covered at a single step. Therefore for the time being one begins with one's own state: what is meant by knowing the far by means of the near. If one state takes effect, the world is easily transformed. Formerly Yao made his capital at Pingyang, Shun held the hundred offices, Tang had seventy li, and King Wen a hundred li; all were ancient rulers who wished to make the luminous virtue clear throughout the world, and who came from the power of vow? Hence I say the 'wish' is the power of vow. The person is the root of the world, the state, and the family. The sutra text afterward always comes back to rest in cultivating the person; hence it is clear that cultivating the person is the essential matter. Yet this one matter is the hardest to understand. Could it be that taking this body of blood and flesh and binding it into caution and dignity, like a boy in the presence of his teacher, is enough to govern a state? Could it be that making every matter on the body look well, like a player on a stage, is enough to bring peace to the world? Hence cultivating the person is spoken of entirely in terms of the mind. Take Yan Hui's asking about benevolence: Confucius told him that to overcome oneself and return to propriety is benevolence; this is precisely the true picture of cultivating the person. Then he told him: if for one day one overcomes oneself and returns to propriety, the world will return to benevolence. This is precisely the true business of governing the state and bringing peace to the world. If one does not believe that this overcoming of oneself is the true business of cultivating the person, how could it be that when Yan Hui asked for its particulars Confucius told him the four prohibitions? Moreover the four prohibitions are all matters of cultivating the person: overcoming oneself is the work of benevolence in the ground of mind; to overcome oneself for benevolence is to manifest the luminous virtue; the world returning to benevolence is to renew the people. 'Benevolence proceeds from oneself' — this self is the true self, namely the place of the highest good. Hence Yan Hui destroyed his cleverness, dismissed his limbs, and practiced the fasting of the mind and sitting in forgetfulness; all these came from the actual effect of the self and are the place of the highest good. What obstructs a person's one body is nothing but seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving: the seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting that are the old knowledge and vision of everyone from ancient times to the present. For benevolence one must cut away utterly all the old knowledge and vision and begin a wholly new life; one cannot enter by carrying along the views of old habitual habits. For the old seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are all contrary to propriety, disordered and inverted, and of no use whatever. Hence, gouging out the heart and plucking out the gall, he brought forth the single character 'do not.' 'Do not' is a word of prohibition, expulsion, and driving out: it means that the old seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting are all to be wholly cut off, with no transgression permitted; to transgress again is to be a thief.
