This is the strictest of prohibitions. Yan Hui heard it and understood at once, and thereupon destroyed his cleverness, dismissed his limbs, and did away with all of it; he simply sat, and sitting he forgot, until he forgot to the place where there was nothing left to forget. Then he turned over and leaped up, and all his seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving were wholly unlike those of the man of former days, as though he had newly built and made for himself another human body. Is this not a new person? Being new himself, he then extended this newness to transform the people, and none of the people failed to be transformed and renewed. This is what is meant by: if for one day one overcomes oneself and returns to propriety, the world returns to benevolence — precisely the effect of cultivating the person. Were it not so, how could cultivating the person be the root of governing the state and bringing peace to the world? The mind is the substance and the host; intention is deluded thought and pondering and is the guest — this is the distinction between mind and intention. Now to rectify the mind one must first cut off at once all the pondering and deluded thought beneath the root of intention, like cutting tangled silk; when not a thought arises, the substance of mind is pure and one without delusion. Hence it is called the thief: the mind's crookedness comes from the intention's insincerity; now that the ground of intention is without delusion, the mind is rectified of itself. Hence it says: wishing to rectify the mind, first make the intention sincere. Knowing and intending are again the distinction between the true and the false. Intention is deluded thought; knowing belongs to true knowing. True knowing is the luminous virtue of the substance, which has always been obscured by deluded thought so that it cannot show through; hence true knowing is dimmed and wronged while deluded thought holds sole power — like a treacherous minister holding the Son of Heaven hostage to command the feudal lords. Now to behead the treacherous and depraved, one must request the sword of the imperial presence; without the true mandate one cannot break the usurper. Hence it says: wishing to make the intention sincere, first extend the knowing. Knowing is the true lord, which has always been confused and unaware. Now the word 'extend' is like 'reach': as when a loyal minister, resolved to remove a traitor, dares not act on his own, but must first bring the traitor's crimes to the knowledge of his lord and awaken him — hence it is called extending. If the true lord once awakens, the treacherous and depraved cannot allow themselves to work their mischief. Hence it says: wishing to make the intention sincere, first extend the knowing. Things are outer things, what has always stood opposed to me — the objects grasped by seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, by seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting. Knowing is true knowing, the originally luminous light of wisdom of the self-substance. This single character 'knowing' is the source of delusion and awakening: because of delusion, inwardly true knowing is transformed into deluded thought, and so the intention is insincere; being insincere, there is no clarity. Outwardly one grasps the true realm as desirable, and so things are not transformed; not being transformed, they become obstructions. Thus this single character 'knowing' is the root and source of inner and outer mind and realm, of the true and the false, of delusion and awakening. The ancients said: the one character 'knowing' is the gate of all wonders and the gate of all calamities. Now, to set aside disorder and return to order, one must inwardly rely on the power of true knowing to break deluded thought, and outwardly use the illumination of true knowing to melt deluded realms. 'Investigate' is the investigate of Yu's investigating the Sanmiao: I move them by utmost sincerity, and they are transformed and return to me — what is meant by utmost sincerity piercing metal and stone and moving pigs and fish. Moreover knowing has true and false, differing, so its use also differs, and investigation likewise has two kinds. Using deluded knowing with deluded thought, things and I stand opposed and obstructive: this investigate is the investigate of grappling and opposition, as when it is said one forms schemes with what one meets and daily does battle with the mind. Using true knowing with utmost sincerity, things and I respond and communicate: this investigate is the investigate of responsive investigation, as when it is said to investigate what is not the mind. Take the donkey's braying, the frog's croaking, and the grass before the window: all are realms of sound and form that stand opposed to me as obstructions. Yet among the Song Confucians there were those who awakened on hearing the donkey bray and the frog croak, or on seeing the grass before the window. Sound and form are one and the same; what formerly stood opposed to me as an obstruction has now been transformed into the wondrous realm of my mind. Things transformed into knowing and made one with me — as a responsive investigation, what doubt remains? Question: true knowing has no thing to oppose it; how does it respond to and investigate things? Answer: true knowing is in fact thoroughly clear within and without, with no thing to oppose; and the principle of responding to things is the hardest to put into words. The Yi says: quiescent and unmoving, yet responsive and thereby penetrating the affairs of the world. Quiescent and unmoving is the substance of knowing; the affairs of the world are outer things; being responsive and thereby penetrating is investigating things. 'Responsive penetration' does not mean that true knowing drills into things, because true knowing is utterly empty and no thing stands before it. The true and false mind and realm cannot both stand: outer things are like darkness, true knowing like the white sun; when the white sun rises, all darkness is at once extinguished. It is spoken of at the point of dissolution and transformation as responsive penetration. When darkness responds to brightness, brightness becomes darkness; now when brightness responds to darkness, darkness departs of itself and brightness stands alone; hence though there is response, the two fundamentally do not meet, and the weight lies with the brightness. The substance of things is originally empty, and only because of deluded grasping do they become obstructions. Now with true knowing illumining alone, the place of release is thoroughly clear, and no thing can confront the feelings. With the quiescent unmoving true knowing one penetrates the illusory things that are originally nothing; thus knowing illumines itself without waiting to respond, and things melt of themselves without waiting to be penetrated; the two do not dissolve each other. How subtle, how subtle! Hence the student values true knowing alone: once true knowing stands, the luminous virtue is luminous of itself, with not a hair of fabrication. This is why the work of the Great Learning speaks of making luminous and of knowing, while cultivation, regulation, governance, and peace are all its things.

Question: In the opening outline you explained manifesting the luminous virtue, loving the people, and resting in the highest good, which are plainly three matters; now in the items you only explain making the luminous virtue clear throughout the world, and it ends by returning to extending knowing and investigating things, as though it were one matter. What does this mean? Answer: This intent of the sage is most wondrous, and no one in a thousand ages has understood it. Among these eight matters, weight is placed solely on the one character 'knowing.' This knowing is the luminous virtue; it is the substance. It was said above that the first 'luminous' has two meanings. What I earlier explained as extending knowing and investigating things uses the former meaning of awakening to clarity, and the work already lies within knowing where to rest: the character 'rest' is the quiescent unmoving substance of knowing, and the 'knowing' of knowing where to rest is the first 'luminous,' which is the work. This passage has already known to the utmost extreme; once the substance of knowing is ultimate, the full business of making the intention sincere, rectifying the mind, and cultivating the person is finished. Thus manifesting the luminous virtue and renewing the people are plainly two matters. Now, wishing to make the luminous virtue clear throughout the world uses the second meaning of displaying and making bright; hence extending knowing and investigating things may also be spoken of in terms of renewing the people. Moreover, knowing where to rest and then having stability is already standing: knowing where to rest, one's own footing is already set firm. Considering and then being able to attain is already reaching: one has penetrated all affairs and things without omission, and before one's eyes there is not a hair of obstruction, so that every dharma is true — is this not already reaching? The reason for standing and the reason for reaching both rely on the power of true knowing. Therefore, in doing the work of renewing the people, one extends the true knowing one has awakened to into all things; and once all things receive the single illumination of my true knowing, they are like snow touched to a red-hot furnace, like frost melted by the blazing sun, transformed without being expected to transform. Hence it says: extending knowing lies in investigating things. Things transform of themselves, and so it is called investigating. Once those things are investigated, my luminous virtue naturally shines throughout the world, and the people renew themselves without being expected to renew. This is what is meant by establishing others and reaching others. Thus manifesting the luminous virtue and renewing the people are but one matter: the three guiding principles are one and yet three, three and yet one. Hence these eight matters only complete the single sentence about making the luminous virtue clear throughout the world. And that one proceeds from family and state and afterward reaches the world is knowing the far by means of the near; this is most clear. Question: how can investigating things bring peace to the world? Answer: just say what the things investigated are. They are heaven, earth, and the myriad things, all contained therein. Could one set aside heaven, earth, and the myriad things and seek out another thing to investigate? If investigating things could not bring peace to the world, why did Confucius say that if for one day one overcomes oneself and returns to propriety the world returns to benevolence? And just say what the world is as a thing, and where returning to benevolence ultimately returns to. Investigate this. Question: how are extending knowing and investigating things reconciled with overcoming oneself, returning to propriety, and the world returning to benevolence? Answer: overcoming oneself is extending knowing; returning to propriety is investigating things; the world returning to benevolence is things investigated. Question: the student does not understand. Answer: the self is the thing; overcoming is extending knowing; returning to propriety means the self is transformed — is transforming the self not investigating things? The world returning to benevolence is a scene of peace beyond compare; this is called things investigated. Question: how are rectifying the mind and extending knowing distinguished? Answer: rectifying the mind is the four prohibitions: first cutting off all that is contrary to propriety in seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting. But it can only cultivate the person and rectify oneself; it cannot transform things. If extending knowing lies solely in investigating things, then one reaches others, and its merit is the greatest; hence the Great Learning places weight on extending knowing. Question: what is the purport of the sequence of investigating things and things investigated? Answer: in the preceding eight matters the character 'first' is used, and the weight altogether falls on the last, extending knowing, which speaks of the work. Now, speaking from things investigated up to bringing peace to the world, the character 'after' is used, and this too raises the character 'knowing,' to show that the seven matters that follow are all the effects of the character 'knowing.' The student must fix his eye on this character 'knowing.' What was said above, that extending knowing and investigating things means responding to things so as to reach one's knowing, uses the investigate of responsive investigation; and what is now said, that when things are investigated the knowing then arrives, means using things to verify the substance of knowing. The meaning is that if those things have even one hair that is not dissolved, then knowing has not reached the utmost; only when things are wholly dissolved is this true knowing brought to its utmost. Thus the investigate of things investigated is the investigate of coming to investigate — the investigate of what is called the coming of the spirits — and is precisely the meaning of the world returning to benevolence. That all things come to investigate is then the effect of knowing. Therefore, with investigating things and things investigated, the student must seek clarity. If all things have come to investigate, then one investigates all the way along until the world is at peace before letting go. The sage's intent is luminously clear; it is only that one must put forth true work before the outcome is seen. Question: from the Son of Heaven down to the common people, all alike take cultivating the person as the root. Since it was said there is only the one character 'knowing,' why does it return to cultivating the person? Answer: if one did not begin the work from cultivating the person, one would not be doing it in empty space. Hence the sage clearly showed you: overcome oneself and return to propriety, and the world returns to benevolence. For the self is one's own person, the thing closest to me, unlike outer things. Overcoming oneself means that in extending knowing I first extend it to the one thing that is my own person. If one investigates this thing that is oneself, and afterward investigates heaven, earth, and the myriad things, what difficulty is there? Hence it is altogether said that cultivating the person is the root. Question: investigate has three meanings: grappling opposition, responsive investigation, and coming to investigate. Answer: the three meanings all issue from one person. Pray let me make it clear by simile. Formerly the wife of Qi Liang was a good weeper. When her husband died she wept for him. At first, when she wept, the neighbors hated the sound and disliked the person, so that hearing her weep they covered their ears and seeing her they shut their eyes, because her weeping was unlike the weeping of others. Yet she did not stop weeping because the neighbors hated and disliked her. After she had wept a long time, the neighbors without realizing it grieved with her and wept too; and weeping, they forgot their dislike. Once dislike was forgotten, their minds turned to pity her. Nor did she stop weeping because they pitied her, but wept on without cease; and after long, everyone in the whole lane was a good weeper. When everyone was a good weeper, they forgot their grief and no longer noticed that anyone was weeping. When everyone weeps well and weeps long, the whole lane makes a custom of it; and once the custom is formed, everyone says he can weep himself. When everyone can weep himself, they look on the wife of Qi Liang as an ordinary woman, no different from themselves, and go about with her in close familiarity, and all is forgotten. Now the wife of Qi Liang wept not for her husband but for her heaven. Heaven is what she depended on all her life; losing it, she could not but weep. Her grief was the regret of a whole heaven. Knowing that heaven would not spare her, her weeping also would not cease; how could it cease because people disliked it? Even if everyone in the whole lane had asked her day after day, her weeping would only be more sorrowful. It was by no means that she meant to have people pity her; how could questioning stop her? Even with a blade before her and a cauldron behind, threatening to stop her, it could not be done. Why? Because beyond this heaven there was nothing to weep for. That at first people hated her was because the pain of her weeping was utterly unlike others': this is grappling opposition. That after long weeping everyone was in pain was because the pain of her weeping cut into people's minds, so that everyone was in pain for himself and not in pain for Qi Liang: this is responsive investigation. And when after long the whole lane became good at weeping until it was a custom, they no longer knew that the pain of weeping came from Qi Liang, and instead looked on the wife of Liang as simply one of themselves: this is coming to investigate. These words, though small, may illustrate great matters.

This is the Resolving of Doubts on the Outline of the Great Learning written by Master Hanshan. The Master dwelt at Caoxi, and scholars with tablets and robes often came with their brushes to ask about the Way. The Master manifested the body of a candidate and taught the Dharma. This year, passing through Wumen, he showed it to Qian Qianyi and said: this old man's playful brush still has a child's heart in it; it is after all not a matter beneath the patched robe. What do you say? I, Qianyi, have heard that Zhang Zishao in his youth studied under Guishan and caught a glimpse of the unarisen middle; and when he came to Jingshan, he was questioned and struck on the purport of investigating things and things investigated, and at once received its subtle meaning. Those who in the late Song were praised for moral integrity all put Zishao first. Seen from today, Zishao's bold arguments at the imperial lecture mat and his late banishment to Hengpu, where he held his book and stood leaning with his legs crossed in hiding — his youthful integrity appears like a goose's footprint in snow and mud. Had he not attained something deep from Jingshan, could he have been so? Those who play Zishao today have different vows, but in proclaiming the right Dharma by means of worldly truth they are one. Bian Que, hearing that the people of Qin loved little children, became a physician of little children. The world today esteems candidates; hence the Master manifests the body of a candidate and teaches the Dharma. How can this be called not a matter beneath the patched robe? Zishao once said: whenever I hear the causes and conditions raised by old man Jingshan, it is like a thousand gates and ten thousand doors opening at a single step. If candidates today can contemplate in this way, the Master's vajra eye will be pointed out one by one from the tip of his brush.
Reverently inscribed with incense by the Yushan silk-capped disciple Qian Qianyi in the fourth month of the dingsi year of Wanli
