blocks.text: A Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi

inline.s: Statement of Intent

The patriarchs of the Western Regions composed treatises to break the non-Buddhists' attachments, and they had to be well versed in their own and others' schools. From ancient times the masters of the sutras and treatises in this land have all been well versed in their own and others' schools; but the last students of our school rest content in their narrow ignorance, are blind to the sameness of substance, look on other teachings as alien things, and cannot interpenetrate the teachings and contemplations, so that they find it hard to benefit the worldly. As for those of initial faith who cannot deeply exhaust the scriptural canon, they suffer from the fragmentation of names and marks and find it hard to comprehend; and as for those who are passionately fond of Laozi and Zhuangzi as a reservoir of style, when it comes to the destination of their words, none fails to gaze at the ocean and sigh. Then, looking at the various commentaries, each follows its own view and is hard to reconcile. And when one sees the Oral Meaning and the Supplementary Ink deeply citing Buddhist sutras, so that every phrase hits the mark, and even saying that the whole great canon issued from this, while the deluded take it as certainly so — one is deeply moved to sigh. Dwelling by the sea, in the leisure left by dry sitting, as I read through the Śūraṅgama and the Lotus, there were those who asked for instruction on the purport of Laozi and Zhuangzi; so the matter ramified to this, and I settled it for myself — not daring to seek understanding from a true man or to make of it a thesis that must be so. Moreover I sigh that those who from ancient times have defended the teaching and broken the enemy mostly dispensed medicine yet seldom opened up the sickness that lies beneath the heart and diaphragm: not that they did not apply it wondrously, but that they had not felt the pulse of the source of the illness. Therefore I have sealed and settled it with the contemplation of mind-only consciousness, like a maṇi jewel's perfect illumination in which the five colors are vividly distinct, like an empty valley transmitting sound to which every echo responds. If one contemplates all dharmas by mind-only consciousness, then they of themselves do not go beyond shadow and echo. Hence the treatise is named after this.
On the Source of the Teachings

I have observed that when the hundred crafts and arts of the world reach their utmost refinement and attain the wondrous, it cannot be transmitted in words; and those who imitate it cannot obtain it in words either. How much less can the wonder of the great Way be conveyed by mouth and ear, by language and letters? It lies in the wonder of the mind's awakening. Thus not only does Chan value wondrous awakening; even worldly cleverness and dialectical acuity, the language of governing the world, and the means of livelihood — there is no single dharma whose wonder is attained without awakening, and what is wondrous cannot be reached by words. Hence when our Buddha, the sage, taught the Lotus he discoursed purely on the true mark; and as for the wondrous dharma, he did not set forth a single word, saying only 'thus.' As for those who awaken to the wondrous dharma, he said only that one who teaches well — the language of governing the world and the means of livelihood and so forth — all accord with the right Dharma. And the sage of the fifth ground in the Avataṃsaka is well able to penetrate the learning of the world; as for yin-yang, the arts of number, charts and writings, seals and tallies, medical prescriptions and verse — there is nothing he does not master. Only then can one enter the world to benefit beings. Hence the great being of Equal Enlightenment manifests forms throughout the ten realms: according to what body and what dharma ought to be used for deliverance, he manifests that body and that dharma and delivers them. Seen in this light, is the Buddha-Dharma utterly without worldly truth, and is worldly truth wholly other than Buddha-Dharma? It is only that people do not awaken to the wonder of the great Way and so draw for themselves the difference of inner and outer. Is the Way really so? I privately observe that those who from ancient times to the present fence off the Way say of this one, 'he is a non-Buddhist,' and of that one, 'he is a heretic.' Seen broadly, they are like prizing and disdaining puppets, drawing boundaries across the great void, or judging the sun and moon by right and wrong. All of them fail to awaken to the wonder of their own minds and merely add to their idle disputation. For the sages of old were nothing else: they were simply those who had awakened to the wonder of mind. All their words and teachings flowed out from the mind of wondrous awakening and were shown according to capacity, shallow or deep. Hence it is said: nothing does not flow from this Dharma-realm; nothing does not return to this Dharma-realm. Therefore, if we do not awaken to our own minds we do not know the mind of the sages; and not knowing the mind of the sages, to imitate the words of the sages is like a player's joy and sorrow: though he rejoices he does not rejoice, though he grieves he does not grieve, for the joy and grief do not come from what he has himself. That joy and grief do not come from oneself yet one takes them as one's own — this I see in those who explain the sages' words.
On the Dharma of Mind

In youth I took Confucius as my teacher without knowing Confucius; I took Laozi as my teacher without knowing Laozi. When grown, I took the Buddha as my teacher without knowing the Buddha. Then I withdrew into the deep mountains and great marshes, practicing stillness to contemplate the mind. Thereby I came to know that the three realms are mind-only and the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Since it is the contemplation of mind-only consciousness, then every form is the shadow of mind, and every sound is the echo of mind. Thus all sages are the tips of shadows, and all words and teachings are the smooth echoes. Because the myriad dharmas are manifested by mind alone, the language of governing the world and the means of livelihood all accord with the right Dharma. Because outside the mind there are no dharmas, every dharma is true; only the deluded cling to them so that they are not wondrous. If one awakens to one's own mind, then no dharma is not wondrous; mind and dharmas are both wondrous. Only the sage can do this.
On Acceptance and Rejection

Our Buddha's sutras all come from the Western Regions and are all from translation. The coming of the sutras began in the Han and became greatly flourishing only in the Western Jin. Among the translators of Jin, Kumārajīva alone is accounted foremost, and his disciples, the four masters Sengzhao, Daosheng, Daorong, and Sengrui, were the unicorns and phoenixes among monks, yet Kumārajīva could employ them. Of Sengzhao, however, Kumārajīva also said: in understanding I do not yield to you; in letters we must bow to each other. For Sengzhao was especially skilled in Laozi and Zhuangzi. Yet the Buddhist sutras all came from the golden mouth's proclamation, and when they reached this land their language was often dissimilar, with some sutras having several translations, so that the shallow-minded doubted. They did not know that the principle is in truth without error; the language lies in the skill or clumsiness of the translator. Hence in the canon, whatever came from Kumārajīva's hand is elegant in style, because he had the four sages at his side. Thus the Lotus is deep in principle and dense in phrasing, exhausting its wonder in every turn without depending on words; and the Vimalakīrti has a style that is graceful and grave, so that its principle is self-evident. As for Sengzhao's four treatises, they are seamless and whole; without the eye of the right Dharma one can by no means understand them. Hence the deluded criticize them, taking them as the reckless talk of the emptiness school and Laozi and Zhuangzi — which is fitting enough for them. The state preceptor Qingliang was a bodhisattva of the Avataṃsaka; when he composed his commentary on the Avataṃsaka he always cited Sengzhao's treatises, and always said 'Master Zhao,' honoring him. I have privately discussed this: if Sengzhao's views were incorrect, how could Kumārajīva have suffered him in the assembly? If Kumārajīva's eye were not clear, how could his translations be honored? If Sengzhao's treatises were not canonical, how could Qingliang have suffered them in his mouth? Through the ages there have been many doubts, yet none has gone as far as this. Why? When we look at the Avataṃsaka commentary, it cites the words of Laozi and Zhuangzi very abundantly, saying: take their style, not their meaning. Guifeng, however, said the two masters cannot trace man to his source, and the Mirror of the School refutes them even more pointedly. Yet all these masters were response-body great beings who raised the great Dharma-banner; why is their acceptance and rejection so at odds? Let me try to discuss it: perhaps each had his own emphasis. For the language of the Western Regions is plain and unadorned and moreover full of repetitions; and where a translator's learning is not good in both languages, the style is often crude and greatly burdens the principle. Now the words of the sages of China, apart from the Five Classics which are bound to the world's teaching, that carry the Way are only the single book of Laozi. But Laozi's words are ancient and terse, deeply hidden and hard to understand, and the one who unfolds the Way of Laozi is Zhuangzi alone. Master Jiao said: Laozi has Zhuangzi as Confucius has Mencius; these words are trustworthy. Yet Confucius called Laozi a dragon; if one met Zhuangzi through Mencius, would one not face him as a disciple? I have sometimes privately said that in China, from the sages down through all ages, those who bear a transcendent view, apart from Laozi, are Zhuangzi alone; and words that carry the Way, vast and free, apart from the Buddhist sutras, among all the philosophers and hundred schools, those that exhaust the study of heaven and man are the single book of Zhuangzi alone. If China had not had this man, through ten thousand ages none would know there is a true man; if China had not had this book, through ten thousand ages none would know there are wondrous discourses. For our Buddha-Dharma is vast and subtle, and translators used perilous phrasing to carry it, so that the principle must be deep and hidden — as in the Laṅkāvatāra. Hence Kumārajīva's translations are accounted foremost because he had the four sages as his support. The state preceptor's saying, 'take their style, not their meaning,' has its reason. If this land had produced words surpassing Laozi and Zhuangzi, Sengzhao would certainly have set them aside. Seen in this light, Sengzhao's use of their style in his treatises and commentaries is because Sengzhao took the Lotus as his school: what is called the good teacher of Dharma, the language of worldly truth, the means of livelihood and so forth, all accord with the right Dharma — the doing of one who has deeply penetrated the true mark. As for Guifeng's slighting and the Mirror of the School's distancing them: Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals, borrowing the command of the heavenly king to carry out reward and punishment; these two masters wielded the authority of the Dharma-king to carry out praise and blame. Qingliang, however, interfused the whole Dharma-realm, having nothing that could not be and nothing that must be; hence he accepted and did not accept. Each had his own emphasis. Hence in the Lotus I see Avalokiteśvara's thirty-two responses, where it says that one who ought to be delivered in the body of a brahmin is shown that body and taught the Dharma; and as for the two sons of Wondrous Adornment, it says your father believed and accepted non-Buddhists and was deeply attached to brahminical dharmas, and the two sons too repented of being born into this house of wrong views. For Laozi and Zhuangzi in this land are of the same kind as the brahmins of the Western Regions. Yet here the Buddha first manifests a body to teach the Dharma and then at once denounces it as the wrong view of non-Buddhists — why? It lies in attachment or non-attachment. Because Avalokiteśvara is perfect and unobstructed, he may manifest a body and teach the Dharma; because Wondrous Adornment was deeply attached, it became the wrong view of non-Buddhists. Hence when the sage teaches people he breaks only their attachment, not their dharma. Therefore all who cling to sound, form, and marks are not of right view.
On Learning and Inquiry

I often see students reading sutras and commentaries, and when they suddenly run into a citation from the philosophers or histories, it is like a tiger blocking the road: they are sure to start back in alarm. And when one teaches them to become familiar with it, they say, that is the talk of an outsider — and turn their heads away. I have also seen gentlemen who take up the words of Zhuangzi and must cite Buddhist words as a mirror, or when a phrase hits the mark, say that the whole great Buddhist canon issued from this. Alas! Can this be called thorough understanding? Weigh these two: to study Buddhism without understanding the hundred schools is not only not to know this dharma but also not to know the Buddha-Dharma; and to explain Zhuangzi while claiming to exhaust the Buddhist sutras is not only not to know the Buddha's intent but also not to know Zhuangzi's intent. This is why it is hard to understand. Hence it is said: one who looks at the small from the great does not see it all; one who looks at the great from the small does not see it clearly. I have often exhorted myself with three matters: not knowing the Spring and Autumn Annals, one cannot engage the world; not knowing Laozi and Zhuangzi, one cannot forget the world; not practicing Chan, one cannot transcend the world. Know this, and one may speak of learning.
On the Vehicles of the Teaching

Someone asked: the sages of the three teachings are originally one principle — is this really so? The answer: if one contemplates by the three realms being mind-only and the myriad dharmas consciousness-only, then not only are the three teachings originally one principle; there is not one matter or one dharma that is not established from this mind. If one contemplates by the equal Dharma-realm, then not only are the three sages originally one substance; there is not one person or one thing that is not manifested by the sovereign power of Vairocana's ocean-seal samādhi. Hence it is said: not destroying marks yet arising dependently, defilement and purity are ever distinct; not renouncing conditions yet being just true, sage and ordinary are equal. Only in what is set up is there the difference of the perfect and interfused versus the progressive, of person and dharma, provisional and real. The perfect and interfused means that all dharmas are but the one mind, with defilement and purity fused and penetrating, without obstruction or hindrance. The progressive means that the ten realms, five vehicles, and five teachings differ in shallow and deep, in principle and practice, cause and fruit. The ten realms are the four sagehoods and six ordinary destinies. The five teachings are the small, the initial, the final, the sudden, and the perfect. The five vehicles are gods and humans, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; the Buddha is the supreme One Vehicle. Yet each of these five vehicles has its own cultivation and advance, its cause and fruit, its ranks and degrees, orderly and without confusion. What is called the human is one between heaven above and earth below, within the four seas, ruled by a sovereign; the root of his cultivation is the five precepts. What is called the god is the gods of the desire realm, ruled by Indra; the root of their cultivation is the ten virtues of the highest grade; the gods of the form realm, ruled by Brahmā, and the gods of the formless realm, sustained by empty samādhi, have as the root of their cultivation the ten virtues of the highest grade together with out-flowing dhyāna and the nine successive absorptions — these two are the causes and fruits within the realm. What the śrāvaka cultivates has the four truths as its root; what the pratyekabuddha cultivates has the twelve links of dependent origination as its root; what the bodhisattva cultivates has the six pāramitās as its root — these three are the causes and fruits beyond the realm. The Buddha perfectly awakens to the one mind and wondrously accords with the three virtues; gathered, they are one, hence the perfect and interfused; scattered, they are five, hence the progressive. This purport is fully recorded in the sutras. Seen in this light, the dharmas of the five vehicles are all Buddha-Dharma, and the practices of the five vehicles are all Buddha-practice; it is simply because living beings' faculties are of greater or lesser size that the sage sets up teachings of shallow and deep, all of it responsive setting-up — what is meant by teaching not overstepping the ranks. From this one knows that Confucius is the sage of the human vehicle, and so he serves Heaven to govern humans; Laozi is the sage of the heavenly vehicle, and so is pure and desireless, leaving the human and entering the heaven. The śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are sages transcending gods and humans, and so rise above the three realms and pass far beyond the four kinds of birth, abandoning gods and humans and not entering them. The bodhisattva is the sage transcending the Two Vehicles, and so leaves gods and humans and enters gods and humans, coming and going in the three realms and saving the four kinds of birth, emerging from the real and entering the conventional. The Buddha is the sage transcending sage and ordinary, and so can be sage and can be ordinary: among gods he is a god, among humans a human, and even among other kinds he divides his form, entering everywhere. Moreover, one who can be sage and can be ordinary — how could sage or ordinary be able to do that? Observed in truth, nothing is not Buddha-Dharma and none of the three teachings is not a sage; whether person or dharma, all belong to the one mind; whether matter or principle, there is no obstruction or hindrance. This is named Buddha. Hence the perfect and interfused does not obstruct the progressive, and the ten realms are manifold; the progressive does not obstruct the perfect and interfused, and the one limit is equal — what division of this and that or dispute of right and wrong could there then be? Hence it is said: whether in the language of the borderlands or in the language of custom, one teaches the four truths. Gods and humans teach the four truths according to custom. Were those two sages not two men secretly sent by our Buddha to be forerunners of the Buddha-Dharma? Thus both the persons and the dharmas are provisional. It is simply that at the gate of establishing transformation one does not destroy the marks of cause and fruit; the learning of the three teachings all guards the student's mind, reaching the deep by way of the shallow and the far by way of the near. Therefore Confucius wished people not to behave as tigers, wolves, birds, and beasts; hence he drew them with benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, for the time being causing them to abandon evil and follow good, to go from being a thing to being a human. He cultivated the teaching of the former kings, made clear the authority of reward and punishment, composed the Spring and Autumn Annals to clarify the traces of order and disorder, rectified people's minds, settled high and low, established the distinctions of ruler and minister, father and son, and fixed the norms of human relations. His methods were strict, his teaching urgent, close to human feeling and easy to practice. But at a time when human desire runs wild, even he, pressing on, found it hard. In my view, had China not had Master Kong, few would have escaped being barbarians or beasts. Yet the traces of Master Kong are indeed thus; was his mind wholly so? Moreover he plainly said: do not be willful, do not be insistent, do not be obstinate, do not be self-centered. Consider his mind of saving the world: was he not one who taught the dharma of governing the world in reliance on the bodhisattva vehicle? That the sutras call him the Youthful Scholar has good reason. But students do not see the sage's mind and think his Way was no more than this; hence they cling to the traces of the former kings to hang up fame and profit, hardening the attachment to self, loosing greed and desire as the burden of life, until some take benevolence and righteousness as capital for robbery and open the calamity of war. Therefore Laozi pitied them, saying: this is the fault of honoring the sages and using cleverness. If one cuts off sagacity and discards cleverness, the people will benefit a hundredfold; if one breaks the measures and snaps the scales, the people will not contend. The harm of greed and desire is extreme. Hence he said: do not display what is desirable, and the mind will not be disordered. Therefore his teaching is to leave desire and be pure, to hold the mind with stillness and stability, not to busy oneself with things, to be tranquil and do nothing — this is the practice of heaven. He causes people to learn this, to leave the human and enter the heaven. Because his words are deep and profound, students find them hard to understand; hence Zhuangzi arose and greatly unfolded them. Because people's clinging is deep, his words were also urgent. As for slandering Yao and Shun and belittling Tang and Wu, these are not grand words but the meaning of cutting off sagacity and discarding cleverness. As for pushing governance back to high antiquity and the Way beyond Fuxi, these are not idle talk but the strongest statement of the harm of doing. As for reviling Confucius, it is not reviling Confucius but reviling those who study Confucius' traces; and moreover they are not literal words but words that break clinging. Hence it is said: nine in ten are fables, seven in ten are repeated words. He denounced teaching and urged separation, destroying form and obliterating cleverness, the intent being to cause people to leave the human and enter the heaven and to remove the burden of greed and desire. As for finely investigating the ways of the world and exhaustively rendering human feeling, breaking the stronghold of the attachment to self and removing the great boundary of human life, with fables spreading out and analogies marshaled in words, incisive and clear, subtle and mysterious, deep and unfathomable — this is one who teaches the dharma of gods and humans and possesses unobstructed eloquence. Is he not one who manifests the body of a brahmin and teaches the Dharma? How is his play so vast? He winnows the dusty world like chaff, sees birth and death as illusion, releases the burden of things, and roams free and easy — how great was his measure of transcendence! I have said that after the usurpations of the five feudal lords, when the unconcerned scholars voiced their arguments across the board and benevolence and righteousness were choked as a road, had not Master Meng arisen and greatly refuted them, the world and later ages would, I think, have worn their garments to the left. In the fury of the many heroes devouring one another, the whole world was dizzy and dim, perishing in things, and many raced after the fire of desire without returning; had this old man not leapt up and bared his arms among them, later ages, even with lofty and pure scholars, would not have known that caps and chariots are fetters. Weighing his merit in saving the world, how great was it? Now his work enters through stillness and stability, and his writing issues from samādhi; but later men peer at the man through the view of one bend and read his book with turbid, disordered minds, so that they are blank and do not know where it tends. If one does not see his mind but observes his words, it is fitting that one is alarmed and does not enter. Moreover he too said: after ten thousand ages, if one meets a great sage who understands his meaning, it will be as a meeting of morning and evening. And that great sage he sought — if not the Buddha, who else? If one takes him as the vanguard of our Buddha in breaking clinging, these words are trustworthy. People of the world do not even enter him; how could they enter the Buddha-Dharma?
On Practice

In our teaching the progressive practices of the five vehicles, though their activities differ, all take calm abiding and insight as the root of cultivating the mind. Hence the calm abiding and insight of our teaching include the Great Vehicle, the Small Vehicle, and the human and heavenly vehicles: the four dhyānas and eight absorptions, and the nine penetrations and clear dhyānas. Confucius also said: knowing where to rest, and then there is stability; and again: from sincerity, clarity. This is the human vehicle's calm abiding and insight. Laozi said: constantly without desire, one contemplates its wonder; constantly with desire, one contemplates its confines. And again: the myriad things all arise together, and I contemplate their return. Zhuangzi also said: nothing is better than clarity; and again: the sage does not go by it but illumines by heaven; and again: no one mirrors himself in running water but in still water; only stillness can still the stillness of others; and again: the great stability holds it. As for the hundred bones and nine openings all complete and present, whom shall I take as kin? And again: all take it for themselves; who then is the angry one? As for the Yellow Emperor's retirement, Yan Hui's fasting of the mind, the old man's catching of the cicada, and Confucius' discourse on dream and waking — these are all works of stillness and stability, releasing form and discarding cleverness, leaving desire and being pure. This is what is meant by loathing the coarse obstruction below and delighting in the pure, wondrous, and separated above, hoping to leave the human and enter the heaven. According to what the teachings make clear, this is one who abandons birth in the desire realm and is born in the first dhyāna. Hence it is said: he whose stability is vast and firm gives forth the light of heaven. This is the heavenly vehicle's calm abiding and insight. The Śūraṃgama says: all in the world who cultivate the mind, if the stain of craving is not produced, do not remain in the desire realm; such a person at a single thought becomes a companion of Brahmā. Again it says: when the habit of desire is removed and the mind free of desire appears, such a person in that hour can practice Brahmā's virtue and is named Brahmā's minister. Again: with pure prohibitions and precepts, together with clear awakening, such a person in that hour can command the hosts of Brahmā and be the great Brahmā king. Again: these three superior classes cannot be pressed by any affliction; though it is not the true cultivation of the true samādhi, in the pure mind the outflows do not stir, and it is named the first dhyāna. As for clarifying the mind until it does not move, limpid and still yet giving forth light, doubling and redoubling its excellence through the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, until subtle seeing appears before one and one molds and casts without obstruction, until one exhausts the ultimate of the group and fathoms the nature of form, entering the boundless and being named the summit of form — this is their realization. Seen in this light, the learning of Laozi, if it says the greatest calamity is none other than having a body, and so extinguishes the body to return to nothing, and that none wearies the form more than having cleverness, and so releases cleverness to sink into emptiness — this resembles the Two Vehicles. Moreover, born in a world without a Buddha, observing transformation and knowing nothingness, he resembles the solitary realizer. His fundamental tenet, emptiness and spontaneity, belongs to the non-Buddhists; but his mind of compassion in saving the world, with gods and humans both returning to him and existence and nonexistence both illumined, again resembles a bodhisattva. Spoken provisionally, he is precisely one who manifests the body of a brahmin and teaches the Dharma. Judged in truth, he is one of the human and heavenly vehicles who finely cultivates the pure life and enters empty samādhi. The reason he can save the world is that the great Brahmā king is the lord of the Sahā world, commanding the world, teaching the ten virtues and saving living beings. According to the Avataṃsaka, the bodhisattva on the grounds is a great Brahmā king, and his Brahmā hosts are all true practitioners among gods and humans, those who cultivate the heavenly practice from the human vehicle; of this kind is he. There is no doubt. Hence I say: the words of Zhuangzi exhaust purely the relation of heaven and man; they are not reckless talk.
On the Basis of Practice

It is from the one mind that the images of the ten realms appear; thus the four sagehoods and six ordinary destinies are all projections of the one mind. How could it be so only for gods and humans? Tracing the ranks of cultivation, they are in truth established from the human vehicle; hence one knows that the human is the root of ordinary being and sage. Therefore Pei Xiu said: ghosts and spirits sink in the suffering of dark sorrow, birds and beasts harbor the grief of fear and flight, the asuras rage, the gods indulge in pleasure; only the human path can order the mind and aspire to bodhi. Seen in this light, apart from the human path there is no way to establish Buddha-Dharma, and apart from Buddha-Dharma there is no way to exhaust the one mind. Thus Buddha-Dharma takes the human path as its foundation, and the human path takes Buddha-Dharma as its ultimate. Hence it is said: what bodhi takes as its object is suffering living beings; if there were no living beings there would be no bodhi. This is what that means. What is called the human path is the relation between ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, and the ordinary affairs of daily life. If ruler is ruler, minister minister, father father, son son, without scheming and without knowing, without greed and without contention, like conjured people, then this is all the superior good people gathering in one place, and this very world is a land of ultimate bliss. What need would there be of sages? Yet human beings are born of craving and die of craving, and their birth, death, and craving are wealth, beauty, fame, food, and sleep. From these five arise greedy, craving minds and the calamity of warring and contention, until ruler is not ruler, minister not minister, father not father, son not son; though the former kings' rewards and punishments were not enough to restrain their minds, they merely satisfied their own insatiable desires and bound up the immeasurable suffering of the future. Therefore our Buddha pitied them, saying: of the causes of all suffering, craving is the root; if craving is extinguished, there is nothing to depend on. Hence he manifested his body in the three realms, sharing the afflictions of the people, and taught the essential path of leaving desire and escaping suffering. And the reason he did not dwell in heaven but was born among humans is precisely to show that the marks of cause and fruit throughout the ten realms are all established from the human path. Since one dwells in the human path, one cannot but know the human path. Hence our Buddha, the sage, did not arise from empty space but took the pure Brahmā as his father and Māyā as his mother, showing that he had ruler and kin; took Yaśodharā as his wife, showing that he had husband and wife; took Rāhula as his son, showing that he had father and son. And he had to leave father and mother and go forth from home — not that he had no ruler or kin, but that he cut off the love of ruler and kin; he cast aside the glory of the state without a backward look, showing that fame and profit are a burden; he threw down wife and child and went far from them, showing the harm of craving; he entered the deep mountains and practiced austerities, showing the practice of leaving desire; he first studied the non-Buddhists' four spheres of totality, showing the leaving of the human and entering the heaven; and he abandoned these and realized the path of universal and perfect enlightenment, showing that the practices of gods and humans are not to be prized. After becoming Buddha he entered the royal palace and raised his father's coffin, and ascended to Trāyastriṃśa to teach the Dharma for his mother, showing that the Buddha-way does not abandon the way of filial piety; he taught the Dharma in dependence on the human world, showing that the human path easily aspires to bodhi; he took kings and ministers as outer protectors, showing that one who dwells in the world does not transcend the ways of the world. These are the models of our great master's manifestation in saving beings, the great norm handed down to later ages. Alas! We who are disciples of the Buddha do not know our Buddha's mind; dwelling in the human world we do not know the affairs of human relations. Discuss Buddha-Dharma with us and we are muddled about true suchness and hazy about Buddha-nature; discuss worldly dharmas with us and we are walled in by every matter, nearly like blockheads; discuss the vehicles of the teaching with us and we say these are branches and leaves, not worth esteeming; speak to us of the six pāramitās and we say the bodhisattva's practice is not something we dare to do; speak to us of the four truths and we say that is the Small Vehicle, not worth doing; speak to us of the four dhyānas and eight absorptions and we say that is what non-Buddhists practice, not worth mentioning; speak to us of the human path and we are utterly blank about the distinctions of ruler and minister, father and son, and the practices of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom. Alas! We do not know what manner of thing we are. Yet we love the high and long for the far, always borrowing from mouth and ear, never knowing that our Buddha saves people and takes them out of the world with the practice of leaving desire as the first of all. Hence it is said: freedom from desire and quiescence is foremost of all. Because I was born on the human path and do not go beyond the human vehicle, in youth I took Confucius as my teacher, knowing that human desire is the root of all suffering. Resolved on the practice of leaving desire, in youth I took Laozi and Zhuangzi as my teachers, contemplating the three realms as mind-only and the myriad dharmas as consciousness-only, and knowing that the ten realms are the projections of mind alone. Therefore I take refuge in the Buddha.
On the Tenet and Tendency

What Laozi takes as his tenet, the great Way of emptiness and nothingness, is precisely what the Śūraṃgama calls the dark and murky emptiness, the luminous essence of the eighth consciousness. For we have deluded this wondrous luminous one mind and made it the eighth ālaya-consciousness; in dependence on this there are the seventh consciousness as the root of birth and death and the sixth as the root of creating karma, transforming and giving rise to the marks of birth and death in faculty-body and world. Thus the sages and ordinary beings of the ten realms all alike do not depart from this consciousness; there is only the difference of broken or unbroken clinging, defilement or purity. Because the ordinary being of the desire realm does not know that the realms of the six dusts and five desires are only consciousness-transformations, he relies on the discriminations of the sixth consciousness, gives rise to greedy, craving minds, and clings stubbornly without letting go, creating all kinds of karma and receiving all kinds of suffering — what is called human desire running wild. Hence Confucius set up benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom as a dike and defense, causing thought to be without depravity and for the time being making people abandon evil and follow good; as for fixing names and ranks and rectifying high and low, his Way does not depart from discrimination. Even the works of stillness and stability he speaks of, verified by consciousness-only, are but the severing of the discriminating, depraved, and deluded thoughts of the first six consciousnesses, so as to remove the harm of contention; and what he ultimately returns to as the wondrous Way takes the seventh consciousness as its place of return — what is called the source of the living impulse, the origin of the Way. Hence it is said: generation upon generation is called the Yi. As for Laozi, who takes emptiness and nothingness as the wondrous Way, he says the valley-spirit does not die, and again that one who dies yet is not destroyed is long-lived, and again that what generates generation does not generate. Moreover his teaching takes cutting off sagacity and discarding cleverness and forgetting form and removing desire as its practice, and takes non-doing as its ultimate tenet. This is a step further than Confucius: he observes the deep pulse of the living impulse, breaks the clinging of discrimination of the first six consciousnesses, subdues the mechanism of arising and ceasing of the first seven consciousnesses, and recognizes the luminous essence of the eighth consciousness — what the Śūraṃgama calls the image-less emptiness, the subtle and refined imagining — taking it as the source of the wondrous Way. Hence he says: dim and vague, within it there is an image; vague and dim, within it there is a thing. Because this consciousness is the whole of ignorance and cannot be seen through by contemplation, he says: remote and dark, within it there is an essence. Because this consciousness-substance perfumes inconceivably and transforms inconceivably, he says: mystery upon mystery, and calls it the wondrous Way. Because heaven, earth, and the myriad things are all manifested from within it, he says: the root of heaven and earth, the gate of all wonders. Not knowing why it is so and yet it is so, Zhuangzi calls it spontaneity. Moreover Laozi was a man of China who had not seen the Buddha-Dharma, and yet his deep observation reached this far; one may call him swift and sharp of faculty. Had he once seen our Buddha and had it sealed and settled, would he not have suddenly realized the true unborn? My thought is that his journey west across the shifting sands was not without meaning. On the whole, this consciousness is deep, hidden, and hard to fathom. When the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world, the ninety-six kinds in the Western Regions took the six masters as their heads; their theses numbered a hundred or more, and there were very many who attained spiritual powers, and their books were more than the Laozi and Zhuangzi of this land. When our Buddha appeared in the world, at the assembly on Vulture Peak the outstanding men were all followers of those six masters. Yet when they saw the Buddha, some awakened without a single word, like a good horse going at the shadow of the whip — was it not that their former practice counted for something, but that the mind of false clinging was not yet forgotten? Hence their seeing the Buddha now was only a matter of a touch that transforms, to break their clinging. Therefore the Buddha's teaching of the Dharma had no redundant words but simply struck and broke them according to the clinging sentiment of living beings, what is called using a wedge to remove a wedge; fundamentally he gave no real dharma to anyone. As for the Śūraṃgama assembly, where he peeled away subtly and disputed in sequence to break the clinging to causality and spontaneity and to cut off the doubts of ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and the Two Vehicles — those who read the teachings do not examine this and merely say, that was a man of the Western Regions; this is a man of the Eastern land. If there is this and that among persons, can the Buddha-nature have two? Moreover our Buddha is the teacher of the three realms and the father of the four kinds of birth; would he teach the Dharma only for the people of that region and have no share at all for those a hundred thousand li away? Yet all living beings, in dependence on the eighth consciousness, have the clinging sentiment of birth and death and hardened self-attachment: is it only the living beings of that region who have clinging and the living beings of this region who have none? Thus this eighth consciousness, the non-Buddhists either cling to it as the dark truth, or as spontaneity, or as causality, or as the spirit-self; and cultivating the mind by stability they are born in the Brahmā heaven and cling to it as the five present nirvāṇas. Or they exhaust emptiness and do not return, entering the formless heaven, subduing the living mechanism of the first seven consciousnesses so that it does not move, and advancing in the contemplation of the nature of consciousness to the sphere of boundless space, the sphere of nothing whatsoever, and up to the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. This is cultivating the mind within the realm without departing from the nature of consciousness. Hence it is said: the student of the Way does not know the true and only recognizes the spirit of consciousness from former times; the root of birth and death through immeasurable kalpas, the fool takes as the original self. This is that. As for the śrāvakas beyond the realm, they have already extinguished the delusions of view and thought in the three realms, already cut off the suffering of birth and death in the three realms, and already realized the bliss of unconditioned quiescence; they do not even know the name of the eighth consciousness, and yet they too take it for nirvāṇa and suppose it the place of ultimate refuge. Moreover they were personally delivered by the Buddha's teaching, and yet it cost our Buddha forty years of rebuke and winnowing; and at the Lotus assembly they still doubted the Buddha's intent, thinking they were saved by the Small Vehicle. Even the bodhisattva on the grounds, having ascended to the seventh ground, only then abandons this consciousness, and still the ripened consciousness is not empty. Seen in this light, the eighth consciousness is the root of birth and death — how could it be shallow? Hence it is said: all in the world who cultivate the path and cannot accomplish supreme bodhi, and even become śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, or become non-Buddhists, gods, Māra kings, and Māra's retinues, all do so because they do not know the two roots. The first is the beginningless root of birth and death: namely that you and all living beings take the grasping mind as your self-nature. The second is the beginningless nirvāṇa, the original pure substance: namely that your essence of consciousness, originally luminous, can produce all conditions and is what conditions leave behind. This is precisely what that means. Ah! Laozi was born into the human world and appeared in a world without a Buddha, and yet he could exhaust the source of creation and observe this deeply; even his diligent practice was truly no easy thing — he had only not yet broken the pit of birth and death. The ancient worthies said: Confucius aids the precepts, because he is strict in governing the body; Laozi aids stability, because he is refined in forgetting the self. The learning of these two sages is mutually necessary with the Buddha and serves as its use — how could it be in vain? Judged in truth, those who cling to Confucius fall into causality, and those who cling to Laozi fall into spontaneity; in sum they have not departed from the nature of consciousness and so cannot exhaust the one mind. The Buddha transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness; hence he says: fundamentally not causality, not spontaneity — only then is the source of the one mind penetrated. This is the division between worldly and supramundane dharmas. What the Buddha breaks is by no means limited to this; even the supramundane Three Vehicles are all within it. People of the world, seeing only that Zhuangzi slanders Yao and Shun, belittles Tang and Wu, and reviles the followers of Confucius, take it as astonishing. What would they do if they heard the World-Honored One rebuke the Two Vehicles as scorched sprouts and rotten seeds, and grieve over the bodhisattvas of heavy defilement as icchantikas of the Buddha-Dharma? Yet the Buddha's rebuke of the Two Vehicles is not a rebuke of the Two Vehicles but of those who cling to the traces of the Two Vehicles, wishing them to abandon the small and aspire to the great. So too Zhuangzi's reviling of Confucius is not reviling Confucius but reviling those who study Confucius' traces, wishing them to cut off sagacity and discard cleverness. In sum, these are all words that send off sentiment and break clinging. If sentiment is truly forgotten and clinging ended, one will join arms and roam in the land of the wondrous Way, with no leisure even for rejoicing in supreme bliss — what need would there be for muddled confusion? The bodhisattva on the grounds in the Avataṃsaka manifests his body among those who smear themselves with ashes, serve fire, lie on thorns, and pierce themselves with needles, becoming their teacher and elder. Were it not for the Buddha-Dharma, how could they be made to enter the Buddha-Dharma? Hence the banners of clinging of those six masters could not be pulled down without the Buddha; and in my view the grand words of Laozi and Zhuangzi could not be verified and directed without the Buddha-Dharma. Truly these are playful discourses; even venerable scholars cannot free themselves from them. Now, by the contemplation of mind-only consciousness, none of them goes beyond shadow and echo.

The conception of this treatise came about when I was dwelling by the sea, in the winter of the wuzi year of Wanli, begging in the royal city; it came up in a night conversation with the layman Dongguan, who clapped his hands greatly. In the summer of the gengyin year I first put brush to it, and after storing it a long time I had never brought it out. In the winter of the jiawu year, following circumstances in the royal city, I meant to ask instruction of the Grand Astrologer Jiao Ruohou, but it did not come about. The next spring, of the yiwei year, I met with calamity for spreading the Dharma, and the draft had already been left by the sea; so I sent my attendant to search it out from among the torn slips. In autumn I received grace and was sent to Leiyang. Chan Master Daguan, coming from Mount Kuanglu with his staff, waited for me on the river; and in the eleventh month, as I was crossing the river, I met the Master at the Thatched Hut of Traveling and Lodging. Sitting at night I brought this out, and the Master read it once and sighed three times, saying: this is enough to dispel long delusion. He at once ordered his disciple Ruqi to cut it in wood to spread the gift of Dharma, and I firmly stopped him. In the summer of the wuxu year, while I was lodging in Wuyang, keeping the retreat with my disciples within the earthen walls and expounding the purport of the Śūraṃgama for the assembly, my disciple Baoqui saw it and sighed with joy, vowing to exert all his strength to complete it and finish the work. Ah! If one would know the meaning of Buddha-nature, one should observe the causes and conditions of the time. These few paltry words are truly not enough to weigh light or heavy in the Dharma-gate: conceived ten years before and completed ten years after, composed east of the eastern sea and practiced south of the southern sea — how could this be so by mere chance meeting of conditions? The Way and the time — how can they be forced? Yet this was written because of observing Laozi and Zhuangzi; hence the treatise is named after them. Written on the last day of the wuxu year of Wanli by the Daoist Hanshan, Qing, in the Laṅkāvatāra Chamber.

After my illness and the clutter of worldly affairs, I have only recently begun to read the great compilation the Caoxi General Record, together with the Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi and other works, and I am deeply moved to admiration. What is meant by: not knowing the Spring and Autumn Annals, one cannot engage the world; not knowing Laozi and Zhuangzi, one cannot forget the world; not practicing Chan, one cannot transcend the world; and by Confucius being the sage of the human vehicle, Laozi the sage of the heavenly vehicle, and the Buddha the sage who can be sage and can be ordinary, can be human and can be heavenly — sayings of this kind are theses that will not change in a hundred generations. Qiyuan bows his head once more.

blocks.text: Opening Topic of the Commentary on the Dao De Jing

inline.s: Elucidating the Tenet

What Laozi takes as his tenet is the wondrous Way of emptiness and spontaneity. This is precisely what the Śūraṃgama calls the absence of all discrimination, neither form nor emptiness, which Kauṣika and others mistook for the dark truth. This is precisely what is called the dark, empty substance of the eighth consciousness. Because this consciousness is most deeply hidden, subtle, and hard to fathom, nothing but the Buddha is sufficient to exhaust it; turned about, it becomes the great perfect mirror-wisdom. Bodhisattvas know this and break it by calm abiding and insight, yet there is still partial realization. As for the śrāvakas, not knowing it, they take it for nirvāṇa; and the brahmin ascetics of the Western Regions, not knowing it, cling to it as the dark truth. This then they take to be the wondrous Way of emptiness and spontaneity. Hence the sutra says: all who cultivate the path and cannot accomplish supreme bodhi, and even become śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, gods, non-Buddhists, Māra kings, and Māra's retinues, all do so because they do not know the two roots and practice in confusion, like boiling sand and wishing to make a fine meal: though they pass through dust-mote kalpas, in the end they cannot obtain it. What are the two? The first is the beginningless root of birth and death: namely that you and all living beings take the grasping mind as your self-nature. The second is the beginningless nirvāṇa, the original pure substance: namely that your essence of consciousness, originally luminous, can produce all conditions and is what conditions leave behind. This saying, that the essence of consciousness is originally luminous, is precisely Laozi's wondrous Way. Hence he says: remote and dark, within it there is an essence; this essence is most real. Because this substance is utterly empty and utterly great, it is not form; because it can produce all conditions, it is not emptiness. Not knowing that heaven, earth, and the myriad things are all manifested from this consciousness, one calls it spontaneity. Because of inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation, it is called wondrous; because it is most refined and unmixed, it is called real; because heaven and earth may perish but this substance does not perish, and the human body may die but this nature abides forever, it is called eternal; because the transformations of the myriad things all issue from it, it is called the root of heaven and earth, the gate of all wonders. Whenever in his book he speaks of the true, eternal, mysterious, wondrous, empty, and great Way and the like, verify it all by this, and one will have a destination of one's own; otherwise one will be as blank as one who grasps at wind and shadows. Hence this is shown first, and in the writing itself there is no need to repeat it.
Elucidating the Aspiration

In my view, one who reads Laozi and Zhuangzi must first become thoroughly familiar with the vehicles of the teaching, finely penetrate the Śūraṃgama, and fuse and comprehend our Buddha's treatises on breaking clinging, so as not to be deluded by his words. Then, finely cultivating stillness and stability, when the work is pure and ripe and the use of mind subtle, one will see this old man's work as bitter and urgent. Yet one must see truly and really that the body is the root of suffering and cleverness the root of burden, so that one can of oneself destroy form and release cleverness, and only then know this old man's true enjoyment and supreme bliss. One must further see through the affairs of the world one by one and see through human feeling one by one, dwell in the world with an empty heart, with not a hair of obstruction before one's eyes, and only then see this old man's true freedom and happiness, vast and free, plainly a man of no affairs. Then, when one has no choice but to respond to the world, one spends not a bit of strength, and serenely governs by non-doing. Observing what he taught Confucius, one may know this. The book of Zhuangzi is the commentary on Laozi; hence what I call Laozi having Zhuangzi is like Confucius having Mencius. Know therefore that what the two masters say is all true speech and not grand words. Hence he said: my words are very easy to know and very easy to practice, yet no one in the world can know them or practice them. But those in the world who discuss the two masters do not at all apply themselves to the work of their own experience; they only imitate them with literary particles of speech, and so fall far short. Moreover there are those who learn their wild and unrestrained manner, but one does not see any who enter by the work of stillness and stability. This is what is meant by those who know me being few. May those who would draw near to the two masters contemplate in this way.
Elucidating the Practice

In the book of Laozi, expositors have always taken emptiness and nothingness as the tenet, and when it comes to seeking the work of entering the Way they are blank and do not know where to lay hand. Hence in the opening chapter I take the one character 'contemplate' in 'contemplate the nothing' and 'contemplate the something' as the essential of entering the Way, so that students may easily enter. Now the work of contemplation and illumination is the greatest, and the sages of the three teachings all showed it to people. Confucius said: knowing where to rest, and then there is stability; and again: manifest the luminous virtue. Knowing and clarity is the meaning of awakening. The Buddha's calm abiding and insight includes the calm abiding and insight of the three vehicles and of gods and humans, with differences of shallow and deep. Confucius is the human vehicle's calm abiding and insight; Laozi is the heavenly vehicle's calm abiding and insight. Yet though the calm abiding and insight of the three teachings differ in depth, the sickness they undertake to cure is in every case first the breaking of the attachment to self as the first step of the work. For the people of the world all take the single character 'I' as the root of the sickness: whether wise or foolish, worthy or unworthy, they press eagerly into the field of fame, profit, and emolument, scheming for the plans of a hundred generations of descendants, exhausting their wit and cleverness, all of it a scheme for one body. As the Buddha said, of the causes of all suffering craving is the root, and all of it is for the sake of the self. Laozi also said: the great calamity is that I have a body. Because the sage Confucius was the head of the teaching of names, toward students of middle and lower capacity he did not dare speak lightly of breaking the attachment to self; only to Yan Hui did he say 'overcome yourself.' For the rest he spoke only of rectifying the mind, making the intention sincere, and cultivating the person. Yet if the mind is rectified, the intention sincere, and the person cultivated, and one applies this between ruler and minister and father and son, each fulfilling his sincerity, this itself is the Way — what is meant by setting it up for the teaching of names. As for cutting off sagacity and discarding cleverness, the purport of no-self, this is for one's own enjoyment, and he likewise did not dare lightly raise it with others, but only drew the bow without letting the arrow fly. Hence he said: if I were sage in benevolence, how would I dare? And again: do I have knowledge? I have no knowledge. A simple fellow asked me, and I was utterly empty. As for where he exerted himself most for others, he said 'overcome yourself,' and he said 'do not be willful, do not be insistent, do not be obstinate, do not be self-centered.' These four sayings lay bare his very heart and liver. Now the self is my private self; willfulness is the arising mind; insistence is the waiting mind; obstinacy is the clinging mind; self-centeredness is the mind of self. To overcome is to cut off utterly; 'do not' is a word of prohibition. He taught people to cut off utterly the sickness of these four: willfulness, insistence, obstinacy, and self-centeredness. For the sage roams the world with an empty heart, quiescent and unmoving, responding to things as they come and penetrating them in response, using the mind like a mirror: neither welcoming nor sending, so that what comes has nothing to stick to and what goes leaves no trace, body and mind both forgotten, contending with nothing. This is the sage's mind. The reason people in the world cannot be like the sage is only that they have the sickness of these four. Hence they are not free and every movement is suffering. Confucius saw that the root of the world's sickness lay here, and so had people cut it off painfully. This very teaching is the Buddha's and Laozi's tenet of no-self. Moreover the character 'do not' is a work of cutting off, the most ruthless laying on of hand, like the words 'you shall not' in the prohibitions of the legalists, making it absolutely impossible to transgress; once one transgresses, the crime admits no pardon. It is only that students do not know this. As for our Buddha's teaching of the Dharma, though vast and boundless, in sum it does not go beyond breaking living beings' coarse and subtle two attachments to self and dharma. Once the two attachments are broken one ascends the Buddha-ground; that is, the whole canon of the three baskets is the instrument for breaking these two attachments. The attachments broken are the four sicknesses of Confucius, which are still coarse attachments. People of the world do not know this and suppose there is some other mystery. As for Laozi, he goes one step beyond the people of the world, and so he established his words solely on breaking clinging, wanting people to release cleverness and forsake form, to leave desire and be pure. Now the cleverness released is private cleverness, which is willfulness and insistence; the form forsaken is obstinacy and self; the desire left is one's private self. Being pure, one is vast and unobstructed like great empty space, which is Confucius' great impartiality. Know therefore that the mind-dharma of Confucius and Laozi is never out of accord; only their gateways and settings, fencing in and guarding the world's teaching, could not but be so. Confucius was devoted to engaging the world, Laozi solely to forgetting the world, and the Buddha solely to transcending the world. Yet though their ultimate aims differ, in truth their first step alike takes the breaking of the attachment to self as the master, and their work alike enters through calm abiding and insight.
Elucidating Substance and Function

Someone said: the sages of the three teachings all teach people first to break the attachment to self, so that the substance of no-self is the same. Why then do their functions differ as engaging the world, forgetting the world, and transcending the world? Answer: both substance and function are the same; there is only the difference of shallow and deep, small and great. If Confucius truly had a self, that would be but the privacy of one man; how could he engage the world? If the Buddha and Laozi truly renounced the world, that would be self-deliverance; how could they benefit living beings? Know therefore that only by no-self can one engage the world, and only by benefiting living beings is no-self revealed; in truth they are one. When Confucius says: quiescent and unmoving, yet responsive and thereby penetrating the affairs of the world — that is function. Brightness then sincerity — that is substance. Sincerity then taking form — that is function. Mind rectified and intention sincere — that is substance. Person cultivated, family regulated, state governed, world at peace — that is function. Laozi's namelessness is substance; doing by non-doing is function. Confucius says: only Heaven is great, and only Yao matched it — vast, so that the people could find no name for it. And again: he who governed by non-doing — was it not Shun? Moreover he takes Yao and Shun as the ancestors of engaging the world: were they men of name and of doing? Only by no-self does one see the whole world as oneself; hence it is said that Yao and Shun were the same as other men. Because all people are of one substance, the only difference is the obstruction of one's private self. Because people's minds are the same mind, where minds are the same there is no obstruction of form; hence he pressed eagerly at teaching and transforming them in order to order and succor them. This is how by no-self one engages the world. Laozi says: he is always good at saving people, and so there are no abandoned people. With no abandoned people, all may become Yao and Shun; this is how by no-self one can benefit living beings. As for the sayings in his book, he acts but does not lord it over, and when the work is done he does not dwell in it — all take non-doing as the great function of engaging the world; how then was he ever one who forgot the world? As for the Buddha, his substance embraces empty space and his function pervades the sand-grain realms; he manifests bodies according to kind, and says: I accomplish perfect enlightenment within the bodies of all living beings. And again: only when all living beings are saved do I accomplish the Buddha-way. And again: if I could cause one living being to arouse the bodhi-mind, I would rather suffer the pains of hell in my own body and never weary of it. Yet are the living beings he transforms not in the world? Since he enters the world to save beings, is this not engaging the world? Moreover to endure the pains of hell without weariness for the sake of one person — is that not pressing eagerly? If there is no kind in which he does not manifest a body, can there be one fixed name for him? Liezi once said: in the West there is a great sage who is believed without words and transforms without doing. How could he have had a mind to do anything? Know therefore that the three sages' substance of no-self and function of benefiting beings are the same; only the scope of their function differs in size. Because Confucius upheld the ways of the world, he began with one body and extended to family and state and afterward to the world; hence his transformation stopped at China, and he wanted everyone to be Yao and Shun, since Yao and Shun were his ancestors. Because Laozi saw the thinness of people's hearts in his time, he thought of returning to high antiquity and took the Yellow Emperor as his ancestor; hence every phrase he spoke was unlike the ordinary, and because he saw that the great Way is hard to accommodate, he went far away across the shifting sands. As for the Buddha, his teaching covers three thousand worlds, most vast and great, without any selection. As Zisi praised the sage, saying: all who have blood and breath none fail to honor and love him. Know therefore that Confucius' substance and function were never small; he was only confined by the times and circumstances. This is precisely the dharma of responding to capacity, and hence close to human feeling. This is the distinction of substance and function. It is a pity that students of later ages each bind themselves to a teaching: those who study Confucianism are constrained, those who study Laozi are wild, and those who study Buddhism are narrow. This is the fault of students, all of it the harm of clinging to self. If one can truly break the attachment to self with strength, then one splits open the fences and is a great master.
Elucidating the Destination

I have privately thought that if the sage Confucius had not known Laozi he would certainly not have been so joyful, and if he had not known the Buddha he would certainly have been impatient; if Laozi had not known Confucius he would certainly not have said again and again that one governs by non-doing, and if he had not known the Buddha he could certainly not have taken compassion as his treasure; and if the Buddha did not engage the world he would certainly not teach living beings in the world. In my view Confucius and Laozi are transformation bodies of the Buddha. If the followers of later ages who study Buddhism do not know Laozi, they will simply go on gazing into empty space, and every dharma before them will be an obstruction, so that nothing can be liberated. If they do not know Confucius, and take the Buddha-Dharma alone into the world, they will certainly not know the ways of the world and human feeling, and on meeting anyone will speak of the mysterious and wondrous, like selling a dead cat's head, of no use whatever. Hence the patriarch also said: if the teaching does not hit the mark, it is idle talk after all. Therefore the Avataṃsaka says: whether in the language of the borderlands, one teaches the four truths. Thus the Buddha's teaching of the Dharma never merely boasted of the mysterious and wondrous. And to save beings according to custom — is that not Confucius' mind of engaging the world? The sutra also says: the sage of the fifth ground, entering the world to save beings, masters every worldly book and art, medical prescription and miscellaneous treatise, chart and seal, all kinds of dharmas without exception, and only then can he respond to capacity. Hence it is said: the language of worldly truth and the means of livelihood all accord with the right Dharma. Thus Confucianism takes benevolence as its root and Buddhism takes the precepts as its root. As for the saying that filial piety and fraternal duty are the root of benevolence, and the Buddha's saying that filial piety is named the precept — in truth they are one. Seen in this light, is the Buddha utterly without a dharma of engaging the world? Because Confucius drove out the barbarians, his teaching traveled in China alone; the Buddha taught the four truths in the language of the borderlands, and so the barbarians all followed his transformation. This is why the scope of their function differs in size. Know therefore that what the sages of the three teachings share is the mind, and what differs is the traces. To seek the mind through the traces is like measuring the sea with a gourd; to fuse the traces through the mind is like a mustard seed containing space. When mind and traces are both forgotten, the ten thousand streams flow to the source and the hundred rivers are one flavor.

To one who has things, one cannot speak of the Way. The myriad things in their profusion are not existent; it is man who makes them exist. If man did not make them exist, how could the myriad things exist? All who have things must die for things; and he who dies for things is near to losing his humanity. If the man is lost, with whom shall the Way be? Things and man — how extreme it is!

One who forgets things is not sufficient to reach the Way. One who does not have things understands things as empty; and things being empty, there is no need to forget, for they are already forgotten. Yet to say I have forgotten things, I have forgotten things, is to have something that can be forgotten, which is not true forgetting, and so it is said to be insufficient to reach the Way.

One who sinks into emptiness is not sufficient to exhaust the Way. The mind that is not empty is so because of things; when things are empty the mind is empty of itself. Mind empty and things empty: then mind is nothing and yet is; things empty and mind empty: then things are and yet are nothing. If so, what is there to stagnate on? But to insist that emptiness is emptiness and to take emptiness as the ultimate is to sink into emptiness — how could that exhaust the Way?

Forgetting and not forgetting are both forgotten; forgetting is forgotten. Yet to insist on both is hard; to forget forgetting and not insist on both is hard. Ah, how ultimate! Where shall I find one who is without forgetting yet without not-forgetting, without both yet without not-both, to speak with him of forgetting and both?

Now those who reach the Way: abiding in dust they always say movement easily alters the substance; leaving dust they always say stillness easily makes one. What is altered by movement is like a spark struck from stone; what is made by stillness is like water that can be dammed. The stone spark seems to be and the swift current seems to stop. Those who think this way do not penetrate the source of movement and stillness, the root of arising and ceasing.

To be moved by things is to have invited it myself. If there were no self, what could move? See how the long wind drums through heaven and earth, the trees break and the hollows howl — what has that to do with the great void? Hence the ultimate man has no self; he is the utmost of emptiness. Because he is empty, he is unmoved.

The substance of mind is originally true; habit and defilement make it deluded. Hence the essential of forging the Way is simply to govern habit, and the essential of governing habit is purely wisdom. Try observing one who melts ice: where fire prevails the ice melts easily; where wisdom is deep habit is easily exhausted.

I believe and others do not: it is not that others do not believe, but that their faith does not reach it. Others believe and I do not: it is not that I do not believe, but that it is not worth believing. Hence I trust in the mind of faith, and others trust in the words of faith. If the words truly meet the mind, then there is nothing not believed.

A grain's weight shifts the utmost heaviness of a thousand catties; one private thought snatches away the great impartiality one originally has. The private is the film over perfect luminosity, the stem of birth and death. Therefore gain does not lie in the small nor loss in the great; the sage is cautious and fearful in the place where nothing is seen and nothing is heard.

Toiling for profit, toiling for fame, toiling for merit, toiling for the Way: the toil is the same, but what one toils for is different. Hence where there is profit there is no fame, where there is fame there is no merit, where there is merit there is no Way; and one who has the Way, the Way accomplished, lacks nothing.

The fish on dry land does not forget to moisten its companion with foam; the caged bird does not forget to preen its feathers, because having lost its proper state it longs to return. That a man should lose his proper state and not long to return means he is not the equal of fish and birds. How sad!

Those who hasten after profit are urgent; those who hasten after the Way are slow. Profit has savor; the Way has no flavor. He who savors the flavorless turns that slowness into urgency. The flavorless — who savors it? He who savors it is called a true man.

The mind is fundamentally a limpid deep pool; by drawing in the objects before it, it muddies its own nature and gives rise to all manner of murky disturbance, oppression, and torment. Tracing it to its root, the fault lies in attachment.

With one film in the eye, empty flowers riot into being; with one mote clinging to the body, mixed thoughts fly in confusion. Understand that the film is without flowers, and dissolve the dust and cut off the thoughts.

The most fine is the greatest; the most subtle is the most manifest. The fine is easily slighted, the subtle easily overlooked. The multitude does not know this; the sage is cautious. Because of his caution, his Way is great and his merit manifest, and through ten thousand ages he has no fault.

In things there is nothing desirable; it is man who desires them, and so they become desirable. Desire is born of craving, and craving must grasp; grasping must enter, and entering means being submerged, so that the self becomes small and things great, life light and things heavy, the man lost and the thing remaining. The ancients who were good at living did not serve things, and so had no desire; though ten thousand forms were arrayed before them, it was as though the West Beauty sold her charms to deer and elk.

I observe that one who is familiar with tigers and wolves, though familiar, is always afraid, fearing they will eat him; hence he is always afraid. What are sensual desire and lust to a man but tigers and wolves? Yet men grow familiar and even play with them, and when they have eaten their fill their hearts are sweet, and they placidly do not know fear. How excessive! Tigers and wolves eat the body; sensual desire eats the nature.

Sensual desire is without rival in its power over man. Hence it is said: thank heaven there is only one such. If there were a second like it, then among all the people under heaven none could practice the Way. In my view, one who is good at opposing desire is best served by wisdom; aid wisdom by revulsion, for revulsion brings fear, fear brings distance, distance brings indifference, indifference brings forgetting. To one who has forgotten, a form is like a puppet and a flavor like chewing wax — what desire is there?

The difficult is easy, and the easy is difficult. The multitude fears the difficult and neglects the easy; the sage fears the easy and reveres the difficult. Therefore there is no Way he does not make great, no virtue he does not make broad, no merit he does not accomplish, no name he does not establish.

The world all takes merit and fame as immortal, believing they can be won by the mind, and so it wearies the mind; believing they can be won by the body, and so it wearies the body. Yet when the toil is utterly spent, one may not establish them; and if established, they may not be firm. Alas! Apart from the sage, who can make them firm? What is not firm decays; what is firm? What I call immortal is different from this: know that my own immortality is immortal.

He who glories in fame stands on tiptoe for fame; he who glories in rank stands on tiptoe for rank. Since he already stands on tiptoe, what disgrace could be added? Hence it is said: he who stands on tiptoe does not stand. He who does not stand has no root; and with no root, in the anxious scramble of name and rank for gain and loss, what glory is there?

Wealth is not great because of what it stores: where there is storing there is loss, and so it is not great. Honor does not reach its utmost because of its height: where there is height there is lowness, and so it does not reach its utmost. Know therefore that the man of penetration stores nothing, and so his wealth is the greatest; is not high, and so his honor is the utmost.

One who hides his traces is not thereby a recluse: the traces are hidden but the mind is not necessarily forgotten. One who leans on fame is not thereby illustrious: the name is illustrious but the Way is not necessarily manifest. Hence reclusion is not rectitude and prominence is not greatness. What I call hiding and manifesting is different from this: I call hiding in the substance and manifesting in the function. When the substance is hidden, one is vast as the great clarity and the ten thousand realms are still; when the function is manifest, all appears in ordered array and the one Way is equally contemplated. Thus adversity and favor accord with circumstance, and failure and success are one. Ah! He who dwells in this is a true man of greatness.

The command of ruler and father cannot be escaped; how much less the great command? Try observing one who bears a small skill and does not understand the great command: in ordinary life he is disappointed, in his proper lot he feels it a time of rejection; hence his mind leaps and stamps, and in indignation he lodges words to seek favor from the world. Ah, how excessive! To a man of penetration it is like one drunk walking at night and striking his forehead against a pillar, or holding a cloth drum and crying to heaven for rescue. Yet though the cloth drum remains, one who knows fate does not take it up.

To take scheming as secrecy is not secrecy; to take the Way as secrecy is secrecy. I have observed one who works a crossbow: perilously poised, a hundred shots and only a few hits — this is a skilled man; how much more the unskilled? One who is good at the Way can spare things: without shooting, nothing escapes him. Hence his secrecy is the greatest and his strength the utmost.

Heaven and earth revolve, a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations; birth and death have their constancy yet none can fathom it. Not fathoming their constancy, one dies for things and forgets. The sage returns to things, and so he flourishes.

What others cast away I take up. Hence what others possess, I do not possess; what I possess, others do not possess. It is not that others do not possess it, but that not knowing they possess it, they do not possess it. If they knew they possessed it, how would I differ from them?

When dust and grime soil a finger, one must wash it before being content; yet when greed and anger harm the virtue, one does not know to cleanse them away. This is to regard virtue as less than a finger. A finger's defilement harms its life; virtue's harm ruins the nature.

He who bears a heavy load is burdened; he who knows much is wearied. Long burdening injures the form; extreme weariness endangers the mind. Once endangered, the reason it is endangered is that one serves the outside. Therefore he who values life serves the inside and not the outside, follows himself and not others, and sets his will on what endures and not on what perishes.
